articles.title: Decisions About Expressing Subjective States Generalise Across Psychological Domain
articles.authors: Jess Grimmond; Scott Brown; Quentin Frederik Gronau; Guy Hawkins
articles.abstract:
People routinely make decisions about how to express their internal psychological states to the
outside world. These communication choices can systematically influence the meaning observers
extract about the internal states of others. In psychological science, this is frequently observed in
the way people respond to self-report surveys. Quantitative cognitive models of these
communication choices, such as the Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) model, translate
continuous psychological states into Likert-type responses. In doing so, the model can separate
internal experiences (latent states) from preferences for (or against) certain response options in
self-report scenarios. A key assumption of the LASARS model is that response style reflects a
stable individual characteristic that generalises across contexts. The present study tested this
assumption by examining whether response styles remain consistent across theoretically distinct
psychological domains. A sample of 145 adults completed four survey instruments assessing
sensation seeking, thinking styles, dark personality traits, and perceived control. We compared a
model in which response style parameters were estimated separately for each instrument with a
more parsimonious model in which response style was assumed to be identical across all
instruments. Response style parameters exhibited strong cross-instrument correlations, exceeding
the magnitude of correlations observed among latent states. Furthermore, constraining response
style to be shared across instruments produced virtually identical predictions of observed scores
and latent state estimates while reducing model complexity substantially. These findings provide
strong evidence that response style is a stable, domain-general characteristic. They also support
the conclusion that people use similar decision strategies to express their internal psychological
states across the different constructs they may wish or be asked to communicate.

articles.title: Innateness is (still) an orienting principle for language development
articles.authors: Leher Singh; Marisa Casillas; Shanley E. M. Allen; Michael C. Frank; Caroline F Rowland
articles.abstract:
How humans come to acquire language has been a persistent object of philosophical and scientific inquiry, in part because it bears on fundamental questions about the nature of human cognition.
Classically, this field of inquiry has centered innateness as a critical component of language acquisition, traditionally characterizing innate capability in terms of richly specified, biologically endowed linguistic structure, such as Universal Grammar. Contemporary theories have evolved considerably from these earlier formulations and now present several differing candidates for innateness in language. Throughout this evolution, though, questions of innateness have remained central to theories of language acquisition, even as the nature of those questions has shifted in response to new sources of evidence. In this Perspective, we consider evidence from three complementary sources of evidence—linguistic diversity, human social interaction, and language models (LMs)—that together inform the question of what children must bring to the task of language learning. We conclude by identifying desiderata for theories of language acquisition that seek to specify the nature, scope, and explanatory role of innate contributions to language development.

articles.title: Distinct sensorimotor representations during combined action observation and motor imagery
articles.authors: Matthew Scott; David Wright; Nicola Jane Hodges; Justine Magnuson; Sarah N Kraeutner
articles.abstract: The human sensorimotor system can represent actions in the absence of movement, termed motor simulation. These motor simulations can be perceptually (externally) driven through observation of an actor or cognitively (internally) driven through imagining movement. Although there is evidence humans can represent multiple actions simultaneously, whether different motor simulations can concurrently be represented is unclear. We investigated the capacity of the sensorimotor system to simultaneously represent observed (action observation; AO) and imagined actions (motor imagery; MI). Two competing hypotheses were tested concerning whether AO and MI could co-exist or not, The Dual Action Simulation Hypothesis (DASH) and Visual Guidance Hypothesis (VGH), respectively. Fifteen participants completed a functional magnetic resonance imagining (fMRI) study, requiring them to complete four distinct conditions involving imagination or observation of a rhythmical hand tapping action. Conditions involved: AO, AO with a counting task (i.e., with cognitive load), MI, or simultaneous AO and MI of different actions (AOMI). Through representational similarity analysis, AO and MI motor simulations were evidenced in the right ventral premotor cortex, supporting DASH over VGH. Multidimensional scaling of representational similarity data indicated a unique representational pattern for AOMI, differing from AO and MI across different dimensions. Whole-brain analyses were conducted, showing descriptive support for greater engagement of sensorimotor regions during AOMI vs. the summation of independent AO and MI conditions occurred, complementing findings from our representational similarity analysis. While dual motor simulations appear possible, our data suggests that the representational pattern of AOMI is distinct, producing super-additive sensorimotor activity. Neither DASH nor VGH adequately explain these data.

articles.title: Connected or drained? An experience sampling study on informal communication and well-being in hybrid work settings
articles.authors: Alicia Andrea Meier-Ernst; Leonard Reinecke
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Informal communication has been ascribed well-being functions. Yet in increasingly hybrid work settings, where employees work remotely, informal exchanges frequently occur via digital channels and may hinder relational bonds and drain rather than restore employees’ energy. Drawing on Communicate Bond Belong Theory, this study examines whether informal communication enhances or undermines employees’ well-being in hybrid settings by considering its perceived quality, relational benefits, and energy-related costs. Design/methodology/approach: A one-week experience sampling study (26 participants; 549 surveys) captured employees’ everyday communication episodes with co-workers and their subsequent experiences. Mixed-effects models estimated within-person relationships while accounting for between-person differences.
Findings: Episodes that were more informal than usual were associated with higher striving potential (e.g., more pleasantness or meaningfulness). In turn, higher striving potential was associated with more relatedness need satisfaction and a more favorable relatedness-to-energy ratio, though not with energy expenditure. Communication modality did not moderate these associations. However, text-based (vs. audio-visual) exchanges were significantly associated with lower relatedness and energy expenditure, and a higher relatedness-to-energy ratio. Originality: Adopting a situational perspective, this study moves beyond frequency-based and between-person approaches to everyday informal communication. It disentangles message- and channel-related effects and their distinct contributions in the relationship between informal talk and employee well-being. From this novel perspective, the findings provide evidence that informal communication is a resource for employees’ well-being, but can impose demands when it occurs digitally, an aspect that practitioners should recognize when designing informal communication initiatives.

articles.title: Trusting the Machine: Separating Trust in GenAI Authors from Trust in Their Content
articles.authors: Caroline Simpson; Clara Colombatto; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang
articles.abstract: As Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) becomes more sophisticated and widespread, it matters how its perceived humanness affects trust. Previous work shows that anthropomorphism increases an agent’s perceived trustworthiness as an advisor. We asked whether an author’s presentation also affects trust in the information it produces in a non-advisory role. In two experiments, participants read a science communication blog post attributed to an author with varying anthropomorphic cues. They rated the trustworthiness of the author (author trust) and the content (content trust). In Experiment 1 (N = 270), the post was attributed to a GenAI author described with low or high anthropomorphic cues, or to a human expert. The human author, who also differed in implied professional expertise, received higher author trust than either GenAI author. This effect was reliably larger than the effect on content trust. The low- and high-cue GenAI authors did not reliably differ, including in anthropomorphism ratings. In Experiment 2 (N = 148, preregistered), participants chatted with a GenAI chatbot, presented as the author, that used fewer (low condition) or more (high condition) anthropomorphic cues. The high-cue chatbot was rated more anthropomorphic and received modestly higher author trust. No reliable content trust effect was detected, and evidence that the two effects differed was inconclusive. Author and content trust were strongly correlated in both experiments. These results suggest that cues to an author’s humanness may shape trust in the author more than in what it communicates, although the clearest evidence came from comparing human and GenAI authors.

articles.title: Seeing a partner’s gestures in conversation increases referential but not form alignment: Evidence for distinct mechanisms of alignment in co-speech gestures
articles.authors: Sho Akamine; antje meyer; Asli Ozyurek
articles.abstract: People often align with one another’s sentence structures, lexical choices, and co-speech gestures during conversation. Such linguistic alignment has been attributed to both low-level priming and high-level collaborative efforts to establish mutual understanding (grounding). Although the contributions of these processes have been extensively investigated for verbal aspects of language use, their roles in co-speech gestural alignment remain largely unexplored. Here, we manipulated partner visibility in a video-mediated dyadic referential communication game (n = 45 dyads) to examine (i) whether priming and grounding contribute to the two dimensions of gestural alignment: referential and form alignment, and (ii) how lexical alignment relates to gestural alignment. We found that participants produced referentially aligned gestures more frequently when they could see their partner’s gestures than when they could not, irrespective of whether their own gestures were visible to their partner. This pattern provides evidence consistent with priming, but not with the predicted grounding effect. By contrast, visibility had little to no effect on Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)-based gesture form similarity, suggesting that the contributions of priming and grounding may differ between referential and form alignment. Furthermore, lexical alignment was positively associated with the frequency of referentially aligned gestures, even after accounting for control variables. This association is consistent with the possibility that shared conceptualization of referents contributes to gestural alignment. Taken together, these findings highlight that mechanisms underlying alignment may differ depending on the dimensions of gestural alignment and point to distinct roles for priming and shared conceptualization in the alignment of co-speech gestures.

articles.title: iOS Shortcuts as a Free, No-Code Tool for Event-Triggered Experience Sampling
articles.authors: Douglas A. Parry; Tilo Hartmann
articles.abstract: Event-triggered experience sampling prompts in situ surveys when specific behaviors or contexts occur. This approach is valuable for capturing infrequent or context-bound experiences but often requires custom or expensive software. This article describes how iOS Shortcuts, a pre-installed automation feature, can provide a free, no-code alternative for event-triggered surveys on iPhones. Using trigger-action programming, researchers can configure automations that launch survey URLs with embedded contextual parameters when designated events occur. We describe the procedure, outline a workflow of triggers, actions, and embedded variables, and illustrate the approach with worked examples and templates.

articles.title: Tales of Life: Curiosity for Positive and Negative Life Stories of Culturally Close and Distant Others
articles.authors: Esther Niehoff; Marret Noordewier; Malgorzata A Goclowska; Suzanne Oosterwijk
articles.abstract: Personalized stories about others’ life experiences are omnipresent in media, yet we know little about what drives people to engage with such narratives. Across two studies (N = 596 UK adults), we investigated how valence (positive versus negative life event) and cultural distance (experience from someone from a culturally close versus distant country) shape social curiosity. Consistently, participants reported greater curiosity for stories about negative life events, especially when the story’s protagonist was culturally close. Structural equation modelling revealed that the relationship between negative valence and higher curiosity was mediated through greater anticipated insight and – counterintuitive at first sight – greater anticipated distress towards negative stories. At the same time, curiosity for negative stories was attenuated through lower expected enjoyment. These findings suggest that curiosity is driven by anticipated emotional impact of either valence, and have implications for fostering empathy and meaningful engagement in media and public discourse.

articles.title: Supporting Early Career Development Through Volitional Personality Change: A Multi-Layered Evaluation of a Digital Intervention
articles.authors: Sofie Dupré; Bart Wille; Barbara De Clercq; Janne Vanhalst; Joeri Hofmans
articles.abstract: Personality change interventions (PCIs) offer promising opportunities for personal development, yet little is known about how different psychological layers of personality—thoughts, feelings, behaviors, skills, and identity—respond to intentional change efforts. This study addressed that question through a six-week smartphone-based intervention tailored to students' preparation for entering the workforce, an applied setting in which PCIs remain understudied. Final-year undergraduate clinical psychology students (N = 565) participated in one of three interventions designed to enhance resilience, social boldness, or punctuality, with a quasi-experimental control group for comparison (N = 99). Participants in all three conditions showed meaningful growth in the targeted facet, with gains exceeding changes in non-targeted facets, surpassing those observed in the control group, and persisting at the four-week follow-up. Moreover, perceived feasibility of change moderated intervention effectiveness. Finally, participants targeting resilience and social boldness showed significant growth across psychological layers, whereas those targeting punctuality changed primarily in the behavioral and skill layers. The identity layer—representing how participants see themselves—exhibited the smallest degree of change. Collectively, these findings enrich volitional personality change (VPC) theory by illuminating how personality change unfolds across different psychological layers, while also demonstrating the feasibility of PCIs in supporting the school-to-work transition.

articles.title: Age-related underestimation of smartphone screen time
articles.authors: Wenyu Wan; Maria G. Jol; Arko Ghosh
articles.abstract: There is growing evidence that self-reported media use poorly reflects real use, yet self-reports remain the dominant method in media research. Furthermore, the capacity to self-regulate smartphone use intuitively depends on how accurately one perceives that use. Here, we directly compared self-reported and objectively logged smartphone screen time in 304 participants aged 20 to 84 years. We found that reporting bias was strongly age-dependent: older adults underestimated their use while younger adults overestimated theirs. The age-related reporting bias was not explained by working memory performance (2-back task). Working memory did not mediate the association between age and reporting discrepancy. Our findings indicate that self-reported smartphone use carry little information on real use. We highlight the importance of objective measures of smartphone use and the need for understanding mechanisms which distort perceived use.

articles.title: The Dutch Gambling Harms Question Inventory (D-GHQI-12): 	 Development, psychometric properties and test-retest reliability
articles.authors: Suzanne Geurts; Heather Wardle; Ruth van Holst; Mijntje Meijer; Antonius J. Van Rooij
articles.abstract:
Introduction. The Netherlands lacks a standardized Dutch-language questionnaire to measure gambling harms. To address this, the current study aimed to develop and validate a set of questions spanning all gambling harms domains relevant to the Dutch context drawing on existing questionnaires. 

Method. First, the performance of 26 newly developed and translated items, covering eight harm domains, was evaluated. The convergent validity, test-retest stability and adequate content coverage of the item pool were evaluated. Beyond gambling product use and engagement, reference points included the Problem Gambling Severity Index, CBA-MI Reported Financial Wellbeing Scale, Australian Personal Wellbeing scale, and Mental Health Inventory (MHI-5). Secondly, the best performing items were selected for a short form scale, to support a high chance of adoption in monitoring. 

Results. Items performed well across multiple psychometric criteria. They demonstrated high levels of understandability, generally supportive evidence for convergent validity, and satisfactory temporal stability. These items also correlated in expected ways with participation in higher risk gambling products. Based on these results, a choice of the most suitable item from each harm domain was made, to construct the Dutch Gambling Harms Question Inventory (D-GHQI-12). 

Conclusion. The new 12 item Dutch gambling harms scale was constructed around explicit harm domains, verified with international experts and Dutch stakeholders, including those with lived experience of gambling harms. This ensured that most recognised domains, including crime, physical health, mental health, and financial harms, are represented by at least one item in the inventory. Taken together, the D-GHQI-12 offers a domain-balanced, Dutch-validated tool for population monitoring.

articles.title: Inference-Time Self-Guidance for Conversational Safety in Delusion-Related Interactions
articles.authors: David Piterman; Elad Refoua; Hadar Dery; Gunther Meinlschmidt; Ziv Ben-Zion; Kfir Bar; Zohar Elyoseph
articles.abstract:
Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in psychologically sensitive conversations, where repeated affirmation may reinforce delusion-related beliefs and associated risk. Inference-time self-guidance, in which a model generates conversation-specific guidance for subsequent responses without parameter updates, may offer an approach to conversational safety, but its utility in delusion-related interactions remains unclear.
Objective: To develop and evaluate conversation-specific inference-time self-guidance for conversational safety in delusion-related interactions.
Methods: In this preregistered study, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, and DeepSeek V4 Flash completed 16 Psychosis-Bench scenarios under Baseline and three self-guidance conditions: response rules, contrastive examples, and short-horizon consequence simulation. The fully crossed design yielded 192 conversations and 2,304 assistant turns. A separate automated judge scored Delusion Confirmation (DCS), Harm Enablement (HES), and Safety Intervention (SIS) using published Psychosis-Bench rubrics. Analyses compared benchmark-defined Explicit and Implicit risk-cue scenarios and examined whether self-guidance reduced this gap.
Results: Across models, all three self-guidance conditions significantly reduced delusion confirmation and harm enablement and increased safety intervention relative to Baseline (all nine PFDR<.001; dz = 1.10–2.17). At Baseline, explicit risk cues elicited significantly greater SIS than matched implicit cues, whereas cue-type differences in DCS and HES were not significant. Self-guidance did not significantly attenuate the explicit–implicit safety gap after correction for multiple comparisons.
Conclusions: Model-generated inference-time self-guidance improved benchmark-defined safety behavior during standardized scripted escalation without parameter updates. These findings support further evaluation of inference-time self-guidance for delusion-related conversational safety, particularly when risk is communicated indirectly.

articles.title: From use perception to use behavior: Digitally traced smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being in daily life
articles.authors: Krisna Adiasto; Fenne große Deters; Lisanne Sarah Pauw; Katharina Salo; Anne Milek
articles.abstract: Research on smartphone use and psychological well-being has yielded ambivalent and generally small effects. Three methodological limitations contribute to this inconsistency: studies typically capture smartphone use through aggregate measures such as screen time, rely on self-reported estimates that are systematically biased, and focus predominantly on between-person differences while neglecting within-person dynamics. The present study addresses these limitations by examining the between- and within-person associations between digitally traced smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being. Using device logged app use data from a 10-day ecological momentary assessment study of romantic couples (N = 342 individuals), we examined five smartphone use purposes – active social use, passive social use, news consumption, entertainment, and practical use – in relation to positive affect, negative affect, and perceived stress. Analyses were replicated across two subsets to circumvent the dyadic structure of the data, and as an internal robustness check. Across both subsets, associations between digitally traced use purposes and well-being were overall modest and largely inconsistent. The only robust finding across subsets was a within-person association suggesting that days of higher than typical active social use were associated with lower positive affect. Notably, passive social use, which is among the strongest negative predictors of well-being in self-report studies, showed no reliable association under device logged measurement. Overall, these findings suggest that the psychological consequences of actual smartphone use behavior are more limited and more context-dependent than self-report studies imply, underscoring the importance of measurement methods in research on digital technology and well-being.

articles.title: Why Computational Cognitive Science? Specifying Social Science Theories as Cognitive Agents
articles.authors: Dohyun Ahn
articles.abstract: Social science theories about how people and environments change each other are mostly stated in words. Verbal statements leave open the quantities and functional forms needed to derive outcomes. Tests of association cannot distinguish the individual rules that could have produced an association, and causal structures established separately are rarely combined. Computational cognitive science offers a remedy: it specifies theories as rules that generate individual judgment and choice, runs the rules, and checks before data collection whether rival rules can be distinguished. Cognitive agent modeling adapts this practice to theories of person–environment relations. Four causal structures recur in social science: the environment changes people, people select their environments, the two change each other over time, and environmental effects differ across people. Cognitive agent modeling specifies these structures as four components of one agent: learning, choice, feedback, and individual differences. The article compares the approach with other computational approaches and works through media effects theories as a case, giving an example specification and four propositions. In a simulation, three rival explanations of crime viewing and fear yielded positive mean correlations, and a design alternating assigned and freely chosen exposure identified the generating specification in 96% to 100% of data sets.

articles.title: Self-report and administrative adversity measures can have divergent associations with adult cognition: Evidence from 10 years of data
articles.authors: Nicole Walasek; Stefan Vermeent; Willem Frankenhuis
articles.abstract: Adversity research typically relies on self-report or aggregates of administrative data, rarely combining measures from both data sources over time. Here, we leverage Dutch administrative data and self-report measures to enable fine-grained, longitudinal tracking of individuals’ environments over a decade. We examine associations between five adversity dimensions—neighborhood threat, unpredictability in neighborhood threat, crime victimization, material deprivation, and health issues—with executive functioning and working memory in two adult samples (N = 1,024; N = 737). Self-report and administrative measures were only moderately correlated, suggesting they capture partially distinct adversity facets. We find that associations with cognitive outcomes mainly occur for neighborhood-level measures. Critically, although associations with administrative and self-report measures converged for some cognitive outcomes, they diverged for others. Specifically, self-reported adversity predicted intact or lowered performance, while administrative measures predicted intact or enhanced performance. These findings highlight the importance of illuminating the effects of adversity through multiple lenses.

articles.title: Cheaper vegetarian meals reduce unhealthy add-on purchases without compensatory spending
articles.authors: Adéla Plechatá; Cecilie Fenja Strandsbjerg; Yanzhen Luo; Kristian Steensen Nielsen
articles.abstract: Price interventions are proposed to promote sustainable diets, yet real-world spillover effects are rarely tested. In three university canteens (94,740 transactions), one lowered vegetarian and increased meat buffet prices for 15 weeks. Unhealthy add-on purchases fell 1.09 percentage points relative to controls, a 26% relative reduction. Cheaper vegetarian lunches involved comparable portions and no more add-ons than meat lunches. We find no evidence that price differentiation shifts unhealthy consumption elsewhere.

articles.title: “I shape my world around my sensitivities”: Auditory environments and sound sensitivity in intermittently-/non-speaking autistic adults
articles.authors: Rebecca Poulsen; Ari Angel Star-McKenzie; Tim Chan; Melanie Heyworth; Liz Pellicano; Diana Weiting Tan
articles.abstract: Auditory environments shape autistic people’s everyday experiences and quality of life (QoL). However, existing literature tends to characterize these experiences primarily as ‘hypersensitivity’, lacking nuance in how everyday auditory environments shape lived experience. Studies focusing on the experiences of autistic people who are intermittently-/non-speaking are also scarce. This study examined auditory experiences in the presence or absence of competing background noise, operationalized through noisy and quiet everyday environments, among intermittently-/non-speaking and speaking autistic adults. 419 autistic adults (Mage=32.2 yrs, SDage=11.3) completed an online survey including a bespoke questionnaire on everyday sound experiences and a sound-related QoL measure. Of these participants, 383 (91%) predominantly used speech while 36 (9%) were intermittently-/non-speaking. Open-text responses from intermittently-/non-speaking participants were analyzed using content analysis. Statistical analyses revealed that intermittently-/non-speaking participants reported greater sound-related impacts on QoL, greater difficulty in quiet environments, and elevated pain hyperacusis compared with speaking participants. Content analysis contextualized these findings: participants often sought predictable environments to support regulation. Adaptive strategies, including selective withdrawal, preparation, and environmental modification, were framed as proactive self-regulation. Together, the findings position sensory accessibility as an environmental design consideration rather than an individual burden, while centering autonomy in managing auditory input to foster inclusion and wellbeing.

articles.title: Tracking the Integration of Novel Words into the Mental Lexicon: Evidence from Mouse Movement Trajectories
articles.authors: Andrew P. Lucas; Richard J. O'Connor; Kevin J. Riggs; Shane Lindsay
articles.abstract: This study investigated lexical competition effects in novel word learning using mouse tracking methodology. We conducted two experiments examining how and when novel word representations become lexicalised, focusing on their ability to engage in competition with existing lexical entries. In Experiment 1, we used mouse tracking to conceptually replicate Weighall et al.’s (2017) eye tracking study, examining lexical competition between newly learnt word–referent pairs and familiar words both immediately after learning and following overnight consolidation. Mixed-effects analyses demonstrated immediate lexical competition effects for novel words. Competition did not differ significantly between words learnt on the previous day and those learnt on the day of testing. Experiment 2 demonstrated that displaying the referent associated with a newly learnt phonological competitor increased immediate lexical competition, even when targets in both conditions had trained phonological neighbours. The temporal dynamics of mouse trajectories revealed that familiar words produced earlier and larger peak competition effects compared to newly learnt words. These findings support models of word learning that allow for rapid lexical integration, while acknowledging that newly formed lexical representations may not immediately exhibit the same processing characteristics as well‑established words.

articles.title: Trail Making Tests in Extended Reality: A Critical Review with Implications for Cognitive Ageing
articles.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis
articles.abstract: Extended reality (XR) versions of the Trail Making Test and Color Trails Test are promising for assessing and training cognition in older adults. However, each XR adaptation is a new instrument, whose display, interaction technique, timing rules and layouts may change what it measures. This critical narrative review maps these implementations by software lineage and appraises their evidence for assessment and training against common criteria. The Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), whose source code was inspected, serves as a measurement case. XR trail-making tests showed convergence with paper and computerised versions, varying by test part and sample, and clinical group differences (e.g., Parkinson's disease, mild cognitive impairment). However, gaps in reliability (e.g., randomised forms), validation (e.g., norms, prospective samples) and reporting (e.g., error handling, build identity) emerged, and no training benefit attributable to the trail-making component was identified. The TMT-VR case shows how interaction technique, timing rule, error handling and unlogged layouts shape a score's meaning. Future tests should log layouts and events, estimate alternate-form reliability and undergo prospective validation, and training trials should isolate the trail-making component. Several XR trail-making tests have moved beyond feasibility, and reported tolerability during supervised sessions supports further evaluation in older adults.

articles.title: Five Platform Functions and the Frustration–Aggression Pathway: A Mechanism Model of Grievance Identity Formation among Young Men
articles.authors: Johan G.L. Verheyden
articles.abstract: Aggression research holds that aversive experience raises aggressive readiness, but whether aggression is enacted depends on appraisal, cue exposure, reinforcement, and inhibition. This theory article specifies how digital platforms may modulate that pathway for young men exposed to identity-relevant status threat. It disaggregates platform effects into five functions: a social comparison amplifier, an identity threat accelerator, a cue-saturated environment, a reinforcement architecture, and an aggression affordance system. Each maps onto a component of the General Aggression Model, cognitive neoassociationism, or I³ Theory, and each is paired with a discriminant prediction that would count against that function if it failed. The article defines grievance identity as a self-schema marked by central in-group injustice, chronically accessible hostile attributions, legitimised adversarial behaviour, and peer recognition for hostile performance, and distinguishes it from collective victimhood, identity fusion, and ideological commitment. A six-stage pathway links identity-relevant goal blockage to inhibition erosion. The article engages with contested evidence on algorithmic recommendation, the selection-versus-amplification identification problem, and the generalisation gap in precarious manhood research. It reports no data and sets out an empirical agenda and conditions for falsification.

articles.title: The Morality of Partiality: How Relationship Expectations Shape Moral Evaluations
articles.authors: Zuleykha Gasimova; Amiya Shelly Aggarwal; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang; Alexander C. Walker
articles.abstract: While impartiality is often regarded as a moral virtue, acting impartially can violate social expectations and relational obligations, creating tension between competing moral considerations. The present research (N = 3,417) examined how people evaluate partial and impartial actors who prioritized either a socially connected other (family member, friend, or community member) or a stranger in need. Across sacrificial dilemmas and more ecologically valid helping scenarios, partial actors were judged more moral and trustworthy than impartial actors. This preference was strongest when impartial actors failed to prioritize a close (family member or friend), rather than more distant (community member), social tie. Impartial actors were also perceived as less predictable and as fulfilling less of their relational obligations, with these perceptions predicting judgments of their moral character. In Experiment 4, participants themselves exhibited a preference for partiality, with most preferring to help a socially connected other over a stranger in greater need. This preference was stronger when decisions were described as publicly observable rather than anonymous, consistent with reputational concerns influencing helping decisions. Together, these findings suggest that everyday moral judgments reflect not only assessments of adherence to abstract ethical principles but also inferences about individuals’ reliability as long-term social partners.

articles.title: Imagery Instructions Reduce False Memories Across the Visual Imagery Spectrum
articles.authors: Xiaonan Li; Wilma A. Bainbridge
articles.abstract: Visual mental imagery is widely theorized to support memory by enhancing the richness and distinctiveness of encoded representations. However, it remains unclear how imagery ability interacts with different encoding strategies to shape memory performance. The present study examined how encoding modality (imagery vs. verbal) and processing focus (item-specific vs. relational) interact with visual imagery ability to influence veridical and false memory in the Deese–Roediger–McDermott (DRM) paradigm. A total of 173 participants (71 aphantasic participants, 12 intermediate, and 90 typical imagers) completed ten DRM lists under one of four encoding conditions in a 2 × 2 between-subjects design. Our results suggest that true recall did not differ reliably between different encoding strategies, nor was it consistently predicted by Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ) scores, indicating that imagery ability does not broadly determine veridical memory accuracy. In contrast, imagery-based encoding reduced false memories (critical lure recall) compared with verbal encoding across the range of imagery abilities. Notably, individuals with aphantasia, despite reporting greater difficulty implementing imagery instructions, showed comparable benefits from imagery-based encoding. This finding suggests that the mnemonic benefits of imagery-based strategies may not depend exclusively on conscious visual imagery and may involve alternative representational processes. These findings challenge the assumption that imagery vividness predicts memory performance and open new avenues for understanding compensatory encoding mechanisms in aphantasia.

articles.title: Beyond accuracy: extracting reaction-time biomarkers of sustained attention and cognitive flexibility from the UCancellation task
articles.authors: Boris Penaloza; Elnaz Vafaei; Jaap Munneke; Anja Pahor; Susanne M. Jaeggi; Aaron R. Seitz
articles.abstract: Cancellation tasks are widely used measures of attention but are conventionally scored by metrics such as mean accuracy or concentration scores, disregarding the temporal structure of responding. Here, we derive two reaction-time (RT) biomarkers from our tablet-based UCancellation task in 388 young adults: intra-individual RT variability (RTV), a marker of sustained attention, and switch cost, an index of cognitive flexibility from transitions between two different task's target categories. Because consecutive targets are separated by a variable number of scanned distractors, both are confounded by search effort, which we remove with a scanning-load (p) correction framework. RTV behaved as a scored individual-difference measure: correction improved reliability and convergent validity against TOVA low-frequency RTV (n = 373), and a cross-target composite was the most reliable index. Switch cost behaved as a within-task phenomenon whose sign reversed with load—large and positive when targets were adjacent, reversing as scanning load increased—consistent with inhibition of return. Together, these metrics show that RT structure within a brief cancellation task carries attentional information that standard metrics alone does not capture.

articles.title: Global Collective Pessimism: People predict a dystopian future and attribute it to political leaders
articles.authors: Hallgeir Sjåstad; Ann-Cathrin Coenen; Jonas R. Kunst
articles.abstract: Personal optimism is widespread. This research provides cross-cultural evidence for collective pessimism. Across four pre-registered experiments in 40 countries (N = 52,508), people believed it is much more likely that a future dystopian society will materialize than a utopian society. Dystopian predictions were driven not by internal attribution, but by asymmetric external attribution: People believed political leaders in society can exert greater influence on dystopian than utopian world development, and high leader impact was correlationally and causally linked to higher scenario likelihood. Text-based analyses revealed that participants named a political leader nearly twice as often in dystopias than utopias, and such personalized dystopias were considered more likely. Dystopian predictions were stronger among left-leaning individuals and in rich democracies, yet generalized across ideologies and world regions.

articles.title: Norms for Gender-Inclusive Role Nouns in Italian: The GIRN-I Database
articles.authors: Claudia Mazzuca; Chiara De Livio; Marta Mirabella; Guido Giovanardi; Anna M. Borghi
articles.abstract: Finding linguistic alternatives that move beyond the gender binary is increasingly indispensable, especially in languages that enforce gendered categorisations through specific linguistic markers, such as Italian. Indeed, gender-diverse individuals face additional distress associated with perceived invisibility arising from the absence of adequate linguistic forms.  To date, substantial research has been devoted to identifying demographic and socio-political factors underlying preferences for gender-inclusive language. However, far less is known about the cognitive mechanisms that underlie these attitudes. Here, we provide the first Italian psycholinguistic database of role nouns (e.g., nurse, carpenter, teacher) encompassing both gendered (i.e., feminine and masculine) and gender-inclusive (i.e., asterisk and schwa) desinences. Remarkably, this is the first contribution explicitly assessing Italian participants’ dispositions towards gender-inclusive desinences. We asked participants to rate role nouns on nine semantic dimensions, including classic dimensions like familiarity and sensibility and less conventional ones like psychological distance and political relevance. Our findings suggest no clear preference for either of the two inclusive alternatives, both of which are perceived as less familiar and less pleasant than their corresponding gendered forms. We suggest that processing components related to linguistic fluency may also contribute to explaining observed preference patterns. Taken together, our findings underscore the importance of considering semantic and linguistic processing factors, alongside ideological and social variables, when investigating attitudes toward gender-inclusive language.

articles.title: Political Ingroup and Outgroup Cues Condition How Large Language Models Refute Conspiracy Theories
articles.authors: Erin B. Fitz; Kyle L. Saunders
articles.abstract: Despite emerging literature on conspiracy theories (CTs) in human-AI interactions, whether large language models (LLMs) refute CTs and how political identities affect responses remains unclear. Drawing on AI system documentation, positive politeness theory, and motivated reasoning research, we hypothesize that LLMs refute most CTs but adapt responses to the political identities of the user and actor in the claim. In a preregistered study comprising 135,845 conversations, 57 CTs, 21 user-actor political identity condition combinations, and seven OpenAI LLMs, we find that 82% of responses refute the CT and 20% exhibit motivated responding, i.e., acknowledge the user's perspective and affirm their concern. While refutation is more likely for CTs implicating Democrats or Republicans, motivated responding typically accompanies refutation and is more likely when claims involve the user’s outgroup---for example, when a Republican user inquires about a CT involving Democrats, and the model refutes the claim. Although responses to CTs implicating Republicans vary more by user identity than CTs implicating Democrats, the former attenuates response differences between outgroup and ingroup claims. These findings raise broader questions about what it means for AI models to be capable and reliable if LLMs consistently refute conspiracy theories but do so in politically asymmetric ways.

articles.title: Validity and Age Sensitivity of the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality: A Comparison with the Paper-and-Pencil Test in Younger and Older Adults
articles.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis; Dante O’Connor; Sarah E. MacPherson
articles.abstract: The Trail Making Test (TMT) is among the most widely used neuropsychological tests, and its completion times slow with age. The Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR) preserves the sequencing structure of the test but replaces pen movements with head-gaze selection in an immersive environment. However, the convergent validity and sensitivity to age of its English-language version in older adults are unknown. Forty-seven younger (20–38 years) and 44 older adults (64–81 years) completed the paper-and-pencil TMT and the TMT-VR in counterbalanced order. Nine scores were derived per format from Parts A and B: completion times, errors, error-adjusted times, and B−A difference scores. Part A and Part B completion times and error-adjusted times of the two formats correlated significantly in the whole sample, and Part B completion times did so within each age group, whereas errors did not. Older adults performed more poorly than younger adults on completion times in both formats, and the age groups were thus differentiated by both the paper-and-pencil TMT and the TMT-VR. The TMT-VR differentiated the age groups statistically better than the paper-and-pencil TMT on Part B completion times, error-adjusted times and errors, but both formats performed comparably on Part A scores. No paper-and-pencil score distinguished between the groups better than its TMT-VR counterpart. The TMT-VR is therefore a valid immersive adaptation of the TMT, and its advantage in age sensitivity lies in the Part B scores. Future studies should aim for clinical validation in older adults.

articles.title: Memory Overlap Shapes General and Specific Memory Differently in Adolescents and Adults
articles.authors: Merron Woodbury; Sagana Vijayarajah; Margaret Schlichting
articles.abstract: Over time we accumulate many interrelated memories which we draw upon to remember both generalities and specifics of our experience. While both aspects of memory improve through childhood, their maturation into adolescence remains poorly understood. Here, we compared how 39 adolescents (12-13 years old) and 36 adults managed differing levels of relatedness (“overlap”) among learned associations to remember shared (general) and unique (specific) features. Across age groups, greater overlap boosted memory for shared features but hindered memory for specifics. However, adolescents showed a reduced benefit of overlap for shared feature memory, suggesting they generalized across related memories differently than adults. Adolescents were also slower than adults to recognize unique features of highly overlapping memories, consistent with prolonged refinement of specific memory. Our results reveal continued maturation of both general and specific memory into adolescence while demonstrating how the overlaps among our experiences shape what we remember.

articles.title: The Developmental English Lexicon Project (d-ELP): Continuous Word Reading Difficulty Estimates of the 9,961 Most Frequently Printed English Words for US Children
articles.authors: Donald Compton; Jay Rueckl; Laura Steacy; Noam Siegelman; Ashley Edwards; Yaacov Petscher; Nicole Patton Terry; Matthew James Cooper Borkenhagen; Chelsea Starke
articles.abstract: The developmental English Lexicon Project (d-ELP) is a database comprising word reading data for 9,961 of the most frequently printed English words for children, including continuous IRT-based estimates of word reading difficulty, accompanying word characteristics, and raw trial-level data. Data on isolated word reading accuracy were collected from 1,907 children in grades 1-5 across multiple US sites. Each child read a list of words ranging from 250 to 500 items depending on reading skill (less proficient children were often unable to finish the entire list of words), with each list representing the full distribution of word difficulties oversampled for words at the child’s reading level. Each child also attempted 99 linking items representing the full distribution of word difficulties. A total of 631,322 total responses were collected with the average child providing 336. For the final sample of words, the average number of responses per word for the 9,862 non-linking items was 47.14 (range of 10-592) and for the 99 linking items the average was 1681.42 (range of 1083-1907). A Rasch model, with planned missing design, was fit to children’s responses on the word list and linking item responses. This introduction describes the motivation for this project; the methods used for data collecting; the analytic framework used to establish a continuous measure of word reading difficulty across words; descriptive statistics of the relational database and initial behavioral results; and a publicly available search engine providing searchable access to the word difficulty ratings and associated word-level statistics.

articles.title: Cognitive Offloading to Generative AI: A Theoretical Framework for Memory, Metacognition, and Consumer Decision-Making
articles.authors: Chen Chen; Kristy Hamilton; Jacob T. Fisher
articles.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) increasingly mediates product search, evaluation, and choice, consumer cognition is becoming distributed across human–AI systems. This shift challenges a largely unexamined assumption in advertising theory: that persuasion operates through cognitive elaboration within the individual consumer. Drawing on cognitive offloading research from cognitive psychology, we develop the CogOffload framework to explain when consumers delegate cognitive work to Gen-AI and what consequences follow. A seven-stage delegation continuum maps increasing levels of offloading, and a value-based cost-benefit framework identifies its antecedents and the moderators that shape how consumers weigh them. We propose three clusters of outcomes. First, offloading weakens memory for brands and product attributes while strengthening memory for AI-generated summaries. Second, it inflates metacognitive self-esteem and decision confidence, producing AI-induced overconfidence that reduces further information-seeking. Third, effects on decision quality depend on AI reliability: when AI is unreliable, verifying AI recommendations imposes cognitive and emotional costs but can restore impaired memory and recalibrate inflated confidence. Seven propositions and three long-term conjectures extend these effects to consumer autonomy, competence erosion, and brand loyalty. Together, the CogOffload framework positions advertising in the era of Gen-AI as operating within a distributed system of human and artificial cognition.

articles.title: Being Observed by a Tutor Enhances Foreign Speech Production Learning in Video-Mediated Training
articles.authors: Qin Li; Piia Astikainen; Xueqiao Li; Shun Liu
articles.abstract: Social presence, particularly awareness of being observed by a tutor, may enhance learners’ engagement and attention during foreign language practice, but its effects on learning and associated neural activity remain poorly understood. We investigated whether learners’ (n = 32) awareness of being observed by a tutor influences foreign speech learning in a short (11-min) video-mediated listen-and-repeat training for Mandarin words. In the online group, learners knew the tutor could see them, whereas in the offline group, they knew the tutor could neither see nor hear them. Tone production was assessed before, during, and after training, and tone identification before and after training. Electroencephalography and autonomic activity were recorded during training. Tone production accuracy improved from pre- to post-training in the online group only, whereas tone identification improved similarly in both groups. Posterior alpha power increased during training in the offline group but did not change significantly in the online group. Together, these findings suggest that awareness of being observed by a tutor may support foreign language speech production learning in video-mediated settings. The accompanying differences in posterior alpha activity further indicate that the social context of learning is associated with differences in neural activity during practice.

articles.title: Risks and Opportunities in Digital Media Interventions for Youth: A Scientometric Review
articles.authors: Olivia Andrews; Mathilde E. Brons; I. Chaplinska; Peter Nikken; H.M. Koning Ina; Sophie Mary; Carlo Schuengel
articles.abstract:
Youth must navigate both the opportunities and risks associated with digital media. This
scientometric review examined 120 empirical studies on digital media interventions for youth
and used the 4C framework (content, contact, conduct, and contract) to map their thematic focus.
Scientometric mapping techniques were applied to explore keyword co-occurrence patterns and
collaboration networks. Most interventions addressed either risks or opportunities separately
(58.3%), whereas 39.2% combined risks and opportunities within the same 4C dimension. Only
2.5% integrated multiple 4C dimensions. Interventions predominantly focused on content and
conduct, with limited attention to contact and contract, including topics like social interactions,
privacy, digital rights, and commercialization. Collaboration patterns were fragmented, with
researchers working within thematic clusters rather than across them, despite drawing on a
shared conceptual foundation. These findings suggest that current interventions cover only part
of the 4C framework. Future research should encourage more integrated, cross-dimensional
interventions and stronger collaboration among researchers.

articles.title: From Individual Gains to Collective Losses? The Socially Corrosive Path of Generative AI
articles.authors: Markus Langer; Igor Grossmann
articles.abstract: AI tools including generative AI (genAI) and agentic AI promise individual productivity gains, and users experience them as a resource that makes them more capable. However, research documents a robust social evaluation penalty for individual genAI use: people who use genAI, or are suspected of doing so, are judged as less competent, less diligent, and less caring. We argue that these judgments, followed through to their behavioral consequences, outline a socially corrosive path of collective genAI use. Along this path, when people substitute human contact with genAI and devalue what colleagues produce, relational interdependence, metaknowledge, and resulting opportunities for scalable collective intelligence decline, whereas trust erodes through a cycle of concealment, suspicion, policing, and blame. Current technology design and productivity narratives amplify these dynamics. We caution against waiting for genAI use to normalize and propose countermeasures: designing genAI for collective functioning, resisting the productivity trap, and making the social norms of genAI use explicit.

articles.title: Can LLMs Grow Like Children? A Developmental Analysis of Capability Trajectories in Language Model Training
articles.authors: Ran An; Tingting Chung; Klaus Libertus
articles.abstract: Within two years, an infant who can barely lift her head learns to sit, reach, and walk. Developmental science found that this growth is both continuous and phased: skills improve smoothly, yet the pace of improvement changes at identifiable ages, and the field built statistical tools to locate those changes. Language models also transform across training, and whether their capabilities grow smoothly or in jumps is actively debated. The present study argues that the developmental answer applies to artificial learners as well, and that the developmental tools can show it. We apply an analysis pipeline built for infant motor development to the training trajectories of 16 open-source language models, each tested at 27 points during training on five benchmarks. The results mirror the infant findings. Growth is continuous but organized into phases, and transitions cluster at a small set of shared points that are deployed differently across domains. Growth proceeds slowly, then rapidly, then slowly, and models differ reliably in developmental rate. Unlike infants, those rate differences are almost entirely explained by model size. The transitions also survive changes of measurement scale, and on a continuous measure they appear earlier and more sharply than on accuracy. The paper contributes a formal test for phase structure in capability growth, a construct mapping between infant development and language model development, and evidence that phase structure may be a shared property of learning systems.

articles.title: (Phon)aesthetics Beyond Sound: Sociocultural Associations, Aesthetic Appeal, and Perceived Valence in Sign Languages
articles.authors: Theresa Matzinger; Monika Boruta-Żywiczyńska
articles.abstract:
Aesthetic evaluations of languages depend not only on the linguistic signal but also on
language-external factors, notably familiarity with a language and the sociocultural
associations triggered by recognising it. For spoken languages, these factors are hard to
separate, because languages evoking strong cultural associations are usually also familiar. We
used sign languages to isolate the influence of sociocultural associations, testing hearing nonsigners
who were unfamiliar with American (ASL) and French (LSF) Sign Language but
familiar with the associated cultures. Participants rated 64 signs (32 ASL, 32 LSF; half
positively, half negatively valenced) for aesthetic appeal, perceived valence and, once given
the meaning, perceived iconicity. Half of participants were told which language each sign
belonged to, whereas the other half received no such information. Appeal ratings for ASL and
LSF differed only when the languages were indicated: the more participants liked French
relative to US-American culture, the more appealing they found LSF relative to ASL, and vice
versa. No such pattern emerged without this information. Sociocultural associations can thus
shape aesthetic evaluation of a language independently of direct linguistic experience.
Additionally, although participants did not know the signs’ meanings, positively valenced signs
were rated as more positive and, particularly in ASL, more appealing than negatively valenced
signs. This suggests that aesthetic and affective evaluations of signs are closely linked. Finally,
more iconic signs received valence ratings more closely aligned with their actual valence. To
our knowledge, this is the first extension of (phon)aesthetic research to sign languages.

articles.title: Effect of Disclaimers on the Public Perception of AI-Generated Medical Advice: Two Preregistered Survey Experiments
articles.authors: Moritz Reis; Florian Reis; Wilfried Kunde
articles.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used by the public as a source of medical advice, yet they can produce plausible but incorrect output. Disclaimers about the limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) are the most common safeguard and are also anchored in regulatory frameworks such as the European Union's AI Act. Whether disclaimers change how laypeople perceive and act on AI-generated medical advice, however, is unknown. We conducted two preregistered, randomized between-subjects survey experiments with US participants recruited via Prolific (study 1: N = 399; study 2: N = 396). Participants read four simulated dialogues in which a patient received medical advice from an AI tool and were randomized to see a disclaimer below the advice or no disclaimer. Study 1 used the standard disclaimer of a popular chatbot; study 2 used a stronger disclaimer that explicitly highlighted the higher risk of error compared with physicians and required participants to confirm having read it. Participants rated the advice’s empathy, reliability, and comprehensibility and their willingness to follow it. In study 1, the disclaimer did not significantly affect any outcome (all p > .17). In study 2, it did not significantly affect empathy, reliability, or comprehensibility (all p > .19). Willingness to follow the advice was slightly lower with the disclaimer (p = .039), but this effect did not remain significant after correcting for multiple testing. Furthermore, there was no significant difference between the two disclaimers. Disclaimers may thus serve mainly as transparency and liability measures and should not be relied on alone to protect users. Alternatives, such as communicating uncertainty within the response and strengthening AI literacy, deserve evaluation.

articles.title: A Three-Wave RI-CLPM Linking Adolescent Affect and their Engagement with Sustainable Development
articles.authors: Richard Anthony Inman; Sara Ribeiro de Faria; Paulo Moreira
articles.abstract: This study examines reciprocal relationships between affect and engagement and disengagement with sustainable development in a cohort of 580 Portuguese adolescents assessed serendipitously before COVID-19 (ages 12-13), during lockdown (ages 13-14), and approximately one year after lockdown (ages 13-14). Random-intercept cross-lagged panel modelling (RI-CLPM) distinguished stable between-person differences from within-person fluctuations. Adolescents with higher negative affect generally reported lower engagement and higher disengagement. Within individuals, higher-than-usual negative affect before the pandemic predicted greater subsequent disengagement during lockdown. In turn, higher-than-usual negative affect during lockdown predicted greater subsequent engagement. No cross-lagged effects involving positive affect or from engagement or disengagement to affect were statistically significant. The findings suggest that negative affect may precede different responses to sustainable development across contextual conditions. Efforts to promote engagement should therefore consider adolescents’ emotional experiences alongside their circumstances, rather than assume that negative affect necessarily undermines engagement or that evoking it will encourage sustainable action.

articles_hidden.title: Linguistic Markers of Self-Representation Reflect Daily Emotional Experiences in an Expressive Writing Study
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Huang; Claire Whiting; Steven Mesquiti; Sofia S. Baran; Erik C Nook
articles_hidden.abstract: The words people use provide important insights into their emotional experiences. Several measures for tracking emotions through language have been developed, including sentiment (i.e., the positivity and negativity of language) and I-usage (first-person singular pronoun use, thought to reflect negative self-focus). However, emerging research using large language model embedding techniques has quantified not just if people use “I” but how they use it, yielding a measure of self-representation (i.e., how strongly people see themselves as “good” and “able” rather than “bad” and “unable”). This measure tracks mental health outcomes in psychotherapy. Given that emotions and emotion regulation are intimately connected to how we view ourselves, linguistic self-representations may also offer a means for assessing emotional experiences. Here, we examined the associations between participants’ linguistic self-representations and daily emotional experiences in a 14-day expressive writing study (N = 53). Within-person associations showed that on days when participants’ self-representation embedding scores were closer to “good” or “able,” they reported more positive and less negative emotions. At the between-person level, people with self-representations overall closer to “good” experienced lower negative emotional reactivity to expressive writing. These findings suggest that linguistic markers of self-representation hold promise as a tool for assessing emotional experiences, extending prior work linking it to mental health. Translations of these findings could contribute to earlier identification of changes in emotional functioning and provide new ways of assessing metrics of mental health through everyday language.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting the Radius of Trust Problem: Who Counts as “Most People”?
articles_hidden.authors: Anu Realo; Jüri Allik
articles_hidden.abstract: General trust in social surveys is usually measured with a Single-Item General Trust (SIGT) question that asks whether “most people” can be trusted. The concept of the radius of trust challenges this approach by highlighting that trust may vary with the social distance between those who express trust and those who are trusted. This has led to the addition of six specific trust questions to the World Values Survey (WVS) questionnaire since Wave 5, which ask respondents to rate their trust in their family, neighborhood, and people they know personally, as well as in people of another religion, people of another nationality, and people they meet for the first time. Analyzing respondents’ answers to the SIGT and six specific trust items in the Integrated Values Surveys (IVS) dataset (1981-2022) across 88 countries and territories and the three most recent survey waves, we find that trust is a complex construct whose invariant property across cultures is a fixed-length vector composed of the squares of its two components: ingroup and outgroup trust. The phrase “most people” in the SIGT question appears to refer to “familiar strangers”—people whom respondents do not know personally but are likely to encounter in everyday life. It is trust in these familiar strangers, rather than in more distant outgroups, which is most strongly associated with the Human Development Index. This association, however, becomes pronounced only at very high levels of human development.

articles_hidden.title: Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex Causally Supports the Memory Advantage of Reading Aloud
articles_hidden.authors: Lihui Hu; Wenjie Chen; Travis Morgan Seale-Carlisle; Agnieszka Konopka; Manuela Macedonia; Brian Mathias
articles_hidden.abstract: Reading words aloud improves later recognition relative to reading them silently, a phenomenon known as the production effect. This advantage may reflect not only the distinctive sensorimotor information generated by production, but also cognitive control processes that prioritise this information during encoding. Given the central role of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) in supporting cognitive control, we tested whether this region causally contributes to the production effect using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). In a preregistered within-participant study, 40 adults completed three sessions in which TMS was delivered bilaterally to the DLPFC. They received continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS), expected to reduce DLPFC excitability; intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS), expected to increase it; or sham stimulation. Participants then read words aloud or silently before completing an old/new recognition test with confidence and recollection judgements. There was a clear production effect: words read aloud were recognised more accurately and quickly, with greater confidence and more frequent recollection ratings, than words read silently. Crucially, cTBS reduced the accuracy advantage for aloud words relative to sham and iTBS. Exploratory receiver-operating-characteristic (ROC) and unequal-variance signal-detection (UVSD) modeling approaches provided converging evidence that cTBS reduced the memory advantage for words read aloud. Stimulation did not reliably affect responses to new words. These findings provide the first causal evidence that the DLPFC helps make words read aloud more memorable, consistent with a role for cognitive control in prioritising the distinctive information generated by speaking.

articles_hidden.title: Noradrenaline-centric bias in the pupil-linked arousal literature
articles_hidden.authors: Simon van Gaal; Lola Beerendonk; Haoyue Zhang; Tobias H. Donner; Jan Willem de Gee
articles_hidden.abstract: The literature on pupil-linked arousal shows a pervasive bias: it often attributes findings to the noradrenergic locus coeruleus while overlooking other neuromodulatory systems. Here, we quantify the extent of this bias and emphasize that correcting it is essential for refining theoretical models and improving interpretability in this rapidly evolving field.

articles_hidden.title: How to end a nightmare using ocular distress signaling
articles_hidden.authors: Remington Mallett; Norah Wolk; Daniel Morris; Yasmeen Nahas; Cameron Sandell; Karen R Konkoly; Michelle Carr; Ken A. Paller
articles_hidden.abstract: Nightmares trap people in a unique state of helplessness. Whereas fear during wake can be resolved with downregulation strategies, fear during sleep typically coincides with a reduction in the cognitive and social routes to implement them. Here, we report a case in which a dreamer and a technician together overcame both limitations, ending a nightmare in real time. A participant experiencing frequent nightmares was enrolled in a protocol designed to induce lucid dreams (restoring cognition during REM sleep) and enable communication from the dream via eye movements (restoring a social connection). During a nightmare, they gained awareness and used the eye signal as a mayday to request extraction from the dream, all while in polysomnography-verified REM sleep. They were awakened by the technician 34 seconds after the help request and reported immediate relief. At 2- and 4-week follow-ups, lucid dream frequency increased relative to baseline, with lucidity reducing the distress of a subsequent nightmare. Together, these results suggest that real-time dream communication might offer an in somno approach to treating nightmares, a core symptom of PTSD and other psychiatric disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Multidimensional Analysis of Personality Prediction from Electroencephalographic Representations
articles_hidden.authors: Seyed Mahan Mohajerani; Moein Esghaei
articles_hidden.abstract: Associations between personality and resting brain activity have proved difficult to reproduce, leaving unresolved whether electrophysiological information is broadly absent or selectively detectable across personality dimensions. Here, we investigated this question in 254 adults undergoing clinical assessment, examining 15 personality-pattern scales of the Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory–IV using resting-state electroencephalography (EEG). We evaluated eight complementary EEG feature families across four representations of personality scores—continuous, two binary thresholds and ordinal—using nested participant-level cross-validation. Most of the 60 scale–formulation combinations showed little predictive performance beyond chance. The strongest evidence concerned Masochistic scores dichotomized at a base-rate score of 60 (area under the curve, 0.630 and 0.594 across two model-aggregation widths), the only combination meeting the within-formulation false-discovery-rate criterion at both widths in fixed-candidate permutation tests. Weaker evidence emerged for continuous Turbulent scores and thresholded Negativistic scores, while an ordinal Histrionic association was identified in a post hoc three-class analysis. Although particular EEG feature families recurred among better-performing configurations, the exact configurations varied across folds. These findings do not support broadly accurate prediction of clinically oriented personality dimensions from resting EEG. Instead, they reveal modest, selective associations whose detection varies across personality dimensions and their operational definitions. Whether these associations generalize, reflect enduring individual differences or provide clinically useful information remains to be established.

articles_hidden.title: Reciprocal Relationships between Machiavellianism and Workplace Competition: A Six-Year Longitudinal Study
articles_hidden.authors: XIAOHAN XU; Bart Wille; Louisa Vofrei; Sofie Dupré; Jasmine Vergauwe
articles_hidden.abstract: Machiavellianism is linked to workplace competition, yet it remains unclear whether this association reflects personality-driven activity effects, environment-driven reactivity effects, or a combination of both. This study examined the reciprocal relationships between Machiavellianism and workplace competition across six years of early career development among 1,513 Belgian university graduates. Using both Cross-Lagged Panel Models and Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Models, we tested longitudinal activity and reactivity processes at the between-person and within-person levels, respectively. To this end, workplace competition was evaluated using both objective occupational characteristics and subjective perceptions. Regarding activity effects, results showed that higher levels of Machiavellianism at career start positively predicted increases in workplace competition (both objective and subjective), but only at the between-person level of analysis. Additionally, results provided evidence for reactivity effects whereby higher workplace competition predicts increases in Machiavellianism, but only for subjective evaluations of competition and when analyzed at the between-person level. Implications for theory and practice are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: What Drives Leaders to Serve? The Joint and Interactive Effects of HEXACO Personality Traits and Implicit Motives on Servant Leadership
articles_hidden.authors: Justine Amory; Sofie Dupré; J. Malte Runge; Bart Wille
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the channeling hypothesis (Winter et al., 1998), this study examines the role of leaders’ explicit personality traits, implicit motives, and their interaction in predicting servant leadership. Using a dyadic design (N = 219), supervisors completed measures of their HEXACO personality traits and implicit motives, while subordinates rated their servant leadership behavior. Contrary to expectations, neither personality traits nor implicit motives explained unique variance in servant leadership. However, interactions between explicit traits and implicit motives significantly improved prediction. Specifically, leaders high in affiliation motivation were perceived as more servant when they scored high on extraversion and, contrary to expectations, low on agreeableness. These findings highlight the value of considering both implicit motives and explicit traits, as well as their interplay, in understanding servant leadership.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping and Understanding Employees’ Perceived Personality–Work (Mis)Fit: a Mixed-Method Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Sofie Dupré; Jasmine Vergauwe; Bart Wille
articles_hidden.abstract: Although perceived person–environment (P–E) fit has been extensively studied and linked to important workplace outcomes, it has not been examined with the same level of attribute specificity as objective fit. This study addressed that gap by introducing and empirically examining perceived personality–work (mis)fit. Employing a multi-method, multi-informant design with 734 employees and 521 supervisors, we aimed to (a) operationalize perceived personality–work (mis)fit using the too little/too much scale, (b) explore the workplace experiences that shape these perceptions, and (c) examine how they relate to supervisor-rated job performance. We found a high prevalence of perceived misfit, with both deficiency (30%) and excess (42%) commonly reported, while perceived fit was observed across a range of personality trait levels. Thematic analysis revealed that negative experiences associated with perceived misfit extended beyond task performance, encompassing well-being concerns and interpersonal difficulties, with distinct patterns across traits. Finally, perceived personality–work (mis)fit showed modest associations with supervisor-rated job performance. Theoretically, these findings provide insight into how employees experience the fit of their personality at work and highlight the value of examining perceived fit with respect to specific personal attributes. Practically, they inform efforts to better support employees’ fit experiences in the workplace.

articles_hidden.title: Bayesian Treed Regressions for Estimating Heterogeneous Trajectories of Test Scores in Large-scale Educational Assessments
articles_hidden.authors: Mingya Huang
articles_hidden.abstract: In large-scale educational assessment, students’ academic outcomes can evolve over time, due to various effect modifiers. For instance, parents’  education level, a common modifier, has been found to have time-varying effects on children’s test scores, leading to heterogeneous academic trajectories. To model these varying trajectories, parametric models like hierarchical linear models (HLMs) are commonly deployed. While these highly parametric methods are interpretable, their predictive capacities have not been rigorously compared to those of more flexible nonparametric approaches. We present the results of systematic simulation studies and empirical analyses comparing traditional parametric models to Bayesian nonparametric models based on Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART). Our findings indicate that BART-based alternatives can (1) achieve comparable out-of-sample prediction as HLMs, after accounting for individual variability over time; (2) provide a reasonable amount of interpretability and uncertainty quantification; and (3) do not incur much more computational burden. This work contributes to the existing social science literature by demonstrating that Bayesian treed regression methods are viable and feasible alternatives to conventional HLMs for predicting heterogeneous trajectories across time.

articles_hidden.title: Taxing working memory shifts the balance from goals to stimulus-response habits
articles_hidden.authors: Tim van Timmeren; Poppy Watson; Irene van de Vijver; Sanne de Wit
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite our familiarity with the concept of habits, eliciting and measuring habitual “slips of action” experimentally in humans has proven to be difficult. A possible explanation is that participants in psychological experiments actively recruit goal-directed control and therefore make few habitual slips-of-action in the presence of stimuli signalling devalued outcomes. In the current experiment we used the symmetrical outcome-revaluation task in combination with a working memory load in an attempt to tip the balance from goal-directed control to stimulus-response habit. During the instrumental learning phase, participants learned to make a Go response to stimuli signalling valuable outcomes (and points) while not responding (NoGo) to stimuli signalling not-valuable outcomes. During the subsequent test phase, the outcomes signalled by the stimuli were either value-congruent with training (still-valuable and still-not-valuable), or value-incongruent (devalued and upvalued). Participants had to flexibly adjust their behaviour on value-incongruent trials where the stimulus-response association learned during training was no longer appropriate. For half the participants, a concurrent working memory load was imposed during the test phase. In line with our preregistered hypotheses, participants showed evidence for habitual slips of action across two experiments, but those under working memory load showed increased habit tendencies (specifically failures to inhibit prepotent Go responses in the presence of stimuli signalling devalued outcomes). This central finding suggests that a working memory load can be used to reveal habits in humans.

articles_hidden.title: PsyScale Studio: A Guided, Browser-Based Application for Developing and Validating Measurement Scales
articles_hidden.authors: Assis Kamu; Nicholas Tze Ping Pang; Ho Chong Mun
