articles_hidden.abstract: Validating a measurement scale requires a long sequence of analyses, from content validity and item analysis to factor analysis, item response theory, fairness and relations to other variables. These analyses are spread across several programs, and many applied researchers find them difficult to choose, run and report. PsyScale Studio is a free web application that guides users through this sequence. Users describe their study purpose and response format (ten formats, from dichotomous tests to forced-choice and formative indices); the application then builds a purpose-specific roadmap, runs each analysis and explains every result in English or Malay with criteria, references and reporting text. Classical, exploratory and Rasch analyses run in JavaScript. Confirmatory factor analysis, measurement invariance, polytomous item response theory, differential item functioning and cognitive diagnostic models run in R compiled to WebAssembly (webR), using lavaan, semTools, mirt and CDM, while the data stay on the user’s computer. Outputs include an APA-style Word report with references and a reproducibility package with the exact R code and input of each analysis. All 12 comparisons of the JavaScript engine with R (psych, eRm) were within tolerance, and the application’s confirmatory factor analysis reproduced lavaan to four decimals. A simulated 21-item mental health scale with known properties illustrates the workflow; the application recovered its factor structure, weak item and differential item functioning. A second example applies cognitive diagnostic models to Tatsuoka’s fraction-subtraction data. PsyScale Studio is available at https://psyscale-studio.web.app.

articles_hidden.title: From Associations to Theories to an Atlas: Building a Cumulative Causal Science of Autism
articles_hidden.authors: Joshua Ewen
articles_hidden.abstract: Stakeholders are concerned that we have not made as much usable progress in autism research as we would want, given that approximately 100,000 papers have been published concerning the condition over the last 100 years. In this chapter, we identify that usable knowledge in the clinical, policy and support realms refers to causal knowledge. In the first half, we diagnose why this causal knowledge is particularly challenging to achieve within the constraints of psychological and cognitive-neuroscientific research, fields in which we typically have to rely on correlation rather than experimental manipulation. The gap between correlation (the information we have access to) and causation (the conclusions we need to make) is related to a large degree to addressing the likelihood of alternative causal paths that are able to explain the observed correlations, and falsifying these alternative causal paths is a primary key to closing the gap and arriving at causal conclusions. In the second half, we prescribe a falsification-centric approach toward approximating causality combined with a quantification of remaining paths. This aggregation will result in an atlas of evidence for and against causal claims in the condition. This approach focuses on empirical opportunities to empirically falsify “unnatural” constructs important to the various autism causal hypotheses as well as falsification of candidate causal relationships between those constructs. Moreover, we are able to accumulate prior results from the 100,000+ papers prior to planning additional data collection in a way that is independent of contemporaneous or even current assumptions in autism research and in a way that circumvents the working memory limitations of any particular researcher, clinician or advocate.

articles_hidden.title: Peers link conflict-resolution reputation to social and cognitive capacities rather than the capacity to impose costs among Ethiopian forager-horticulturalists
articles_hidden.authors: Zachary H Garfield; Erik Ringen; Edward H Hagen
articles_hidden.abstract: Leadership emergence in socially egalitarian contexts depends on the qualities of individuals and on how others perceive their capacity to use them. Multi-Capital Leadership theory proposes that leaders deploy material, social, somatic, and neural capital to solve problems of group living by providing benefits to group members or imposing costs. Conflict resolution is one important leadership domain. We reanalyse peer rankings of 60 adults in a relatively egalitarian community of Chabu forager-horticulturalists in southwest Ethiopia. Seven peer-raters ranked participants on twelve traits identified as relevant to leadership in contemporary evolutionary theories. A previous analysis averaged rankings before modelling, obscuring differences among raters and treating positions within an ordering as continuous measurements. Here, we fitted a multivariate Plackett–Luce model directly to the individual rankings. This accounts for dependence within rankings and incorporates uncertainty into estimates. It also allows us to estimate consensus orderings and systematic variation associated with rater sex. Male and female peer-raters produced broadly similar orderings, including for conflict resolution. This could reflect actual covariation in participants’ qualities, a shared evaluative schema, or both. Peer-ranked proxies for material, social, and neural capital covaried closely and did not form clearly separable perceptual domains. The clearest descriptive contrast was between benefit-related attributes, including conflict resolution, sound decision-making, and prosociality, and cost-related attributes, including being feared and fighting. Conflict-resolution reputation was most closely associated with decision-making, kin support, respect, and intelligence, and showed no clear positive association with fighting. In these rankings, a reputation for conflict resolution was more clearly distinguished from aggression and coercion than were measures capturing the three capital domains represented in the instrument.

articles_hidden.title: The Cognitive Science of Maria Montessori.
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Desirée Di Paolo
articles_hidden.abstract: Maria Montessori is among the most globally influential figures in the history of education, yet she remains almost entirely absent from the history of science. This paper argues that her absence is unwarranted, and that her work is best understood not as pedagogy but as the empirical investigation of cognitive development by a scientist trained in the positivist and evolutionary milieu of late nineteenth-century Rome. Drawing on Italian-language sources and untranslated early publications, we reconstruct her scientific formation, in particular her relationships with the anthropologist Giuseppe Sergi and the experimental psychologist Sante De Sanctis. We believe that these relationships gave her a theory of cognitive development structured around three irreducible and simultaneous dimensions: individual variation, the designed material environment, and the socio-cultural context. The prepared environment, the central contribution of her method, was designed to make these dimensions explicit and tractable, and maps with notable precision onto frameworks that cognitive science has formalised only recently. We then ask why this scientific dimension of her work has gone so consistently unseen, identifying three historical and contingent causes: a communicative style bent by financial and political necessity, systematic losses in translation, and the structural exclusion she faced as a woman in the scientific institutions of her time. We close with the case of Jean Piaget, whose sustained exposure to Montessori's method, and subsequent formalisation of a developmental theory that diverged from hers on precisely the points where later research has moved back in her direction, offers the sharpest illustration of what the misreading has cost.

articles_hidden.title: Visual Properties of E-Mobility Devices Shape Their On-Road Vulnerability: Effects of Size and Speed
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Wang; Madeline Jarvis; Ella Du Plessis; Ariella Stephen; Blake Jones; Narelle Haworth; Hinze Hogendoorn
articles_hidden.abstract: The brief visual window—often only hundreds of milliseconds—in which drivers predict the arrival of oncoming vehicles and decide whether to give way is critical for safe and efficient manoeuvring. E-mobility devices (EMDs) are a relatively new form of transportation and may challenge these decisions due to their small visual profile and relatively high operating speeds. Here, we examined whether observers show systematic biases when judging EMDs relative to other common vehicles, potentially contributing to their vulnerability in intersection crashes. Using naturalistic video stimuli spanning seven vehicle categories, we tested whether observers would overestimate the time-to-arrival (TTA) of EMDs and, consequently, accept smaller gaps for them to pass through an intersection. Consistent with this prediction, EMDs elicited greater biases in both TTA and gap judgements (N = 31 and N = 59), with these effects further amplified on a visually complex road. By comparing across vehicle categories under naturalistic viewing conditions, the results provide evidence that the amplified biases observed for EMDs arise from differences in the underlying visual signals available to observers—specifically, their smaller retinal size and potentially less reliable motion cues at higher speeds. Importantly, these biases were not explained by speed misperception: in a separate two-alternative forced-choice task (N = 49), EMDs were perceived as faster, not slower, than other vehicles at matched speeds. This dissociation indicates that TTA overestimation cannot be attributed to speed underestimation alone. Together, these findings link controlled psychophysical processes to real-world traffic behaviour, with implications for future experimental design and traffic safety policy.

articles_hidden.title: The case for a developmentally-informed education system in the early years
articles_hidden.authors: Jenny Louise Gibson; Sally Hogg
articles_hidden.abstract: A developmentally-informed early years system is one that is underpinned by a clear understanding of children. In this chapter we argue that this involves integrating scientific insights into child development with expertise in how public policy, services and practices can influence this development. We present a framework of six core principles capturing essential knowledge about child development, which we propose should inform decisions about early childhood education and associated policies and services. We explore these principles in the context of the Early Years landscape in England. We consider challenges for this framework in the current system and explore what might be done to make the whole system – from front line practice to national policy – more developmentally- informed.

articles_hidden.title: A systematic review of implicit statistical learning in schizophrenia spectrum disorders
articles_hidden.authors: karolina.knizkova@nudz.cz; Monika Vecerova; Kateřina Horníková; Mabel Rodriguez; Barbora Kerkova
articles_hidden.abstract: This systematic review examined current findings on implicit statistical learning (ISL) in schizophrenia spectrum disorders and the factors that influence performance. We aimed to update and expand the existing literature by including various ISL tasks, such as serial reaction time, artificial grammar learning, or transitional probabilities. We also considered several ISL moderators related to the characteristics of these tasks, as well as a host of potential clinical and cognitive correlates. We searched PubMed, Scopus, PsycINFO, and MEDLINE Complete for original studies published in English involving adults diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorders. Twenty-one studies published between 1992 and 2025 met the inclusion criteria. We extracted relevant data including study information and design, sample characteristics, ISL task type and characteristics, and main outcomes. Study quality was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Assessment Scale. Findings were heterogeneous, with studies reporting both intact and impaired ISL. The most frequently reported outcome with the largest aggregate patient sample showed that ISL was preserved in comparison to healthy controls. Seven studies reported ISL deficits, and the rest reported mixed or condition-specific findings. The most promising moderators included task and stimulus type. Disorganized symptomatology and working memory span consistently correlated with ISL performance. In contrast, antipsychotic dosage, overall symptomatology, illness duration, or explicit memory did not show consistent associations with ISL.

articles_hidden.title: Gaming disorder assessment tools: A comprehensive systematic review
articles_hidden.authors: Muddsar Hameed; Matthew Stevens; Marcela Radunz; Christina R. Galanis; Sanni Behm; Henrietta Bowden-Jones; Joel Billieux; Simone Rodda; Stéphanie Baggio; Katajun Lindenberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Gaming disorder (GD) is an emerging addictive disorder, comparable to gambling disorder, that has been included in the International Classification of Diseases, Eleventh Revision (ICD-11). Globally, the study of GD has grown rapidly but the research base has been criticized for its inconsistent assessment. This comprehensive systematic review aimed to update two previous reviews (2013, 2020) to evaluate all English-language GD tools and their research evidence. A database search identified 49 tools employed across 1,296 peer-reviewed studies involving more than 2.7 million participants. Tools were evaluated according to: conceptual alignment and practical utility; compatibility with DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 criteria; sample and study characteristics; and psychometric properties. The evaluation showed that the GD field has greatly proliferated across its health subdisciplines and quadrupled in size since 2020. Based on review data from 2013 and 2020, and assuming similar growth and sustainability, the GD field may increase to more than 2,000 studies by 2033. Key findings included: (1) tool coverage of DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 criteria has improved, particularly for assessment of impaired control; (2) instrument choice differs considerably across epidemiological, neurobiological, and treatment research streams; and (3) many tools demonstrate basic reliability and validity indicators, but more rigorous psychometric validation is needed. The GD field would benefit from an international ‘gold standard’ tool to harmonize measurement and generate a more cohesive evidence base. To advance, the field should capitalize on opportunities for innovation in screening to more effectively assess the unique needs, challenges, and characteristics of gaming populations.

articles_hidden.title: Excitation-inhibition imbalance in depression and the limits of observability: cohort-level inference from resting-state EEG with an amortised three-region Wilson-Cowan model
articles_hidden.authors: peng yu; ze yang; Shiqi Zhang; Cui Ruolin; Liu Yijun; cheng kang; lu cao; ning ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Depression is widely thought to involve an imbalance between neuronal excitation and inhibition, but the idea has rarely been tested quantitatively at the level of macroscopic brain networks, because dynamical models are hard to fit to EEG spectra and fitting them person by person is prohibitively slow. We present a complete, reproducible pipeline that makes such a test possible, and we report where it succeeds and where it does not. Using eyes-closed resting-state EEG from 117 participants (22 with lifetime major depressive disorder, 95 without), we fitted a three-region excitatory-inhibitory network model with an amortised Bayesian method, in which a single shared library of simulations serves every participant and reduces inference to milliseconds per person. Depressed participants showed a consistent shift towards excitation in three core networks, together with a stronger inhibitory loop gain and a lower operating-point drive. The model's default-mode resonance frequency rose with symptom severity, whereas the conventional peak-frequency estimate computed from the same recordings did not. We then asked what the model actually buys. For distinguishing groups it did not outperform simple spectral measures, and its per-person low-frequency predictions were poor, so we restrict our claims accordingly. A real-time state observer detected sudden shifts in the network's operating point within milliseconds, yet could not reconstruct the moment-to-moment state, a limit set by the model's intrinsic randomness rather than by our algorithm. Finally, a dose-matched control showed that closed-loop stimulation is no more accurate than a fixed stimulus at the same dose, so we report the real-time feasibility of the loop without claiming an accuracy advantage. The contribution of the paper is therefore a reusable, calibrated inference pipeline together with an explicit map of its limits, including negative findings that we deliberately kept as results.

articles_hidden.title: Individual differences in vision science: The case for a paradigm shift, what it buys, and how to do it well
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Nearly a decade ago, Mollon, Bosten, Peterzell, and Webster (2017) asked what individual differences can teach visual science and what counts as good experimental practice. Studies since then have changed both answers. The study of individual differences is a paradigm, not a technique, with its own objects, standards of evidence, and products. Long practiced in the shadows by a small group, it should move into the mainstream and integrate with existing paradigms, treating differences among observers as evidence rather than error. Its central object is the latent factor, which can earn roles from latent mechanism to established mechanism, computational phenotype, heritable phenotype, endophenotype, or factor-targeted marker, each requiring stricter evidence. Twelve pillars organize what the paradigm buys, including links across domains and levels and tests of whether constructs are unitary. Several 2017 conclusions need correction, above all the definition of true individual differences as stable, long-term traits, and the 2017 prescriptions (rank statistics, required test-retest reliability, fixed test order, mandatory blocking, blanket correction for multiple comparisons) each trade one error for another. Because global artifacts produce general factors, tuned factor structure is itself evidence against them. The long-term goal is a computational atlas of human visual variation: its mechanisms, their sources, and optimal markers for the clinic and for design.

articles_hidden.title: Psychophysiological correlates of fear of movement-related pain assessed during a picture-based paradigm in people with chronic shoulder pain
articles_hidden.authors: Larissa Pagels; Niklas Fengler; Ann Meulders; Waclaw M. Adamczyk; Frédéric Li; Falco Lentzsch; habil. Marcin Grzegorzek; Marcela Camargo Tozzo; Anamaria Siriani de Oliveira; Kerstin Luedtke
articles_hidden.abstract: Fear of movement-related pain (FMRP) contributes to disability in chronic musculoskeletal pain. However, psychophysiological correlates of activity-specific threat appraisal during FMRP-eliciting tasks remain insufficiently understood. This cross-sectional study examined self-reports and psycho-physiological responses to shoulder-straining daily activities in individuals with chronic shoulder pain (CSP) and pain-free controls. Participants observed six pictures depicting shoulder movements select-ed as highly or minimally threatening. Each picture was presented five times in random order. Partic-ipants were informed that they would subsequently perform the activities. Following each presenta-tion, participants rated anticipated fear, urge to avoid, and expected harmfulness. Electrodermal ac-tivity, pupil diameter, heart rate, respiratory rate, and gaze behavior were recorded continuously. Self-reports differentiated between highly and minimally threatening activities and were higher in the CSP group (p≤0.001). SCL differentiated between threat categories, with more pronounced responses in the CSP group (pBH-corrected=0.008; f2=0.029). Within the CSP group, SCL correlated weakly with ratings of fear (ρ=0.137; pBH-corrected=0.008) and harmfulness (ρ=0.127; pBH-corrected=0.013), but not urge to avoid (ρ=0.022; pBH-corrected=0.763). Pupil dilation (pBH-corrected≤0.001; f2=0.039) and gaze be-havior (pBH-corrected=0.006; f2=0.067) differed between individual pictures in the CSP group but did not consistently differentiate the predefined threat categories. Heart rate and respiratory rate showed no consistent effects. This is the first shoulder-specific picture-viewing paradigm combining self-reports with several psychophysiological measures and the first study to examine pupil dilation as a potential correlate of FMRP. The findings suggest that electrodermal activity may reflect sympathetic arousal related to activity-specific threat appraisal during FMRP-eliciting picture-viewing.

articles_hidden.title: The Precision Trap: On the Idealization of Mathematics in Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Sepehrdad Rahimian
articles_hidden.abstract: Calls for greater precision and mathematization in psychology are often motivated by the hope that they will help overcome the field's theoretical problems. While mathematics undoubtedly contributes to scientific progress, this paper questions the idea that an increase in mathematization, in itself, constitutes progress. First, it examines the tradeoffs of precision, arguing that making a theory more precise can change what is being studied, reduce its functionality, and sometimes lend an unwarranted authority to its claims. It also considers examples of non-mathematical yet successful psychological approaches. Second, the paper introduces the Mathematization Bind. Under a realist standard, mathematical precision cannot, by itself, establish that a theory has moved closer to Reality, as the history of the luminiferous aether illustrates. Under a pragmatic standard, the value of mathematics depends on what it enables us to accomplish, relative to the goals of inquiry. Neither perspective justifies treating greater mathematization as scientific progress by default. The paper also questions the tendency to regard an idealized image of physics as the model of scientific maturity. It concludes that the appropriate role and degree of mathematization in psychology should be determined by what it actually contributes to scientific inquiry, rather than by expectations about what a mature science ought to look like.

articles_hidden.title: The Cost of Disconnection: Longitudinal Egocentric Network Analyses Linking Social Isolation to Loneliness and Mental Health in Adolescents and Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Lu Zhang; Alba Bruggeman Nelissen; Sarah Daniels; Matthew Richards; Jack L Andrews; Susanne Schweizer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Social disconnection has been proposed as a contributing factor to the youth mental health crisis. However, it remains unclear how social disruptions reshape social networks and their links to mental wellbeing across age groups. The present study examined whether social disruptions (during the COVID-19 pandemic) reshape social networks and how changes in social networks differently relate to mental health and loneliness in adolescents compared to adults. 
Methods: The study used egocentric network analysis of data from 1,278 participants (88% female; aged 11-89 years, mean = 37.2±16.2 years) in the multinational (Australia, the U.K., and U.S.) prospective COVID-19 Risks Across the Lifespan (CORAL) Study. Social network properties of structural density, functional closeness, and interaction frequency were derived. Linear mixed-effects modelling was employed to examine cross-sectional and prospective associations with mental wellbeing at baseline, three-month, and six-month follow-up.
Results: Adolescents reported more virtual interactions, and less in-person contact. Greater network closeness was associated with lower depression, whereas dense but less close networks were linked to greater loneliness. Reduced contact from pre-pandemic levels were also linked to poorer wellbeing, particularly among younger individuals. 
Conclusions: The present findings highlight that age differences in social experiences, such as social network structure (density) and function (closeness and interaction frequency), may underlie young people’s greater mental health vulnerability during social disruptions. This underscores the importance of developing age-sensitive and context-responsive strategies to better support mental wellbeing during times of social disruption.

articles_hidden.title: Does creative engagement spill over to calculated risk taking?
articles_hidden.authors: Shenghui Xiaoyong; Zhuoqi Yin; Huimin Kong; Kelong Lu
articles_hidden.abstract: Creative engagement may shape not only the ideas people generate but also their willingness to take calculated risks in subsequent decisions, yet this possibility remains underexplored. Across three studies, we examined this relationship and whether general self-efficacy or affective state accounts for the relationship. Study 1 (N = 228) used a cross-sectional survey and found that everyday creative ideation behavior was positively associated with overall and domain-specific risk-taking propensity. General self-efficacy did not mediate this association. Study 2 (N = 83) experimentally compared calculated risk taking after creative drawing versus standard coloring using a binary lottery choice. Creative drawing increased affective dominance but did not significantly influence calculated risk taking. Study 3 (N = 94) compared calculated risk taking after creative writing versus standard typing using a six-level investment-choice task. Creative writing increased both calculated risk taking and affective dominance, but the change in dominance did not mediate the effect on calculated risk taking. These findings suggest that creative engagement can influence subsequent calculated risk taking, although the effect may depend on the creative task and the sensitivity of the risk measure. Neither general self-efficacy nor affective dominance explained this relationship, highlighting the need to investigate alternative psychological mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: The Feasibility of Conducting Research on Cannabis Use in Early Adolescents in England
articles_hidden.authors: Yifan Huang; Leah Fawaz; Amanda Sarpong; Shareha Saiady; Chloe Dagcevizi; Solveig Carer; Kelly Charge; Maria Livanou; Jake Camp; Amy Lineham
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Approximately 10% of early adolescents in the UK report lifetime cannabis use. However, contemporary UK research in this population remains limited due to recruitment, consent and safeguarding challenges. We explored the feasibility of conducting research about cannabis use in UK adolescents aged 13–15 years.

Methods: This exploratory feasibility project comprised an online quantitative survey and qualitative interviews on cannabis use and mental health. Participants aged 13-15 years were recruited through schools, drug services, social media, posters and word-of-mouth. Participants consented through either a standard parent-and-adolescent pathway or an independent Gillick-competent pathway. Feasibility outcomes included total recruitment, cannabis-user recruitment, successful data collection, and the extent of safeguarding actions required. 

Results: 175 participants completed the survey (Mage = 14.35, 54.9% female) and n=13 (7.4%) reported lifetime cannabis use. 16 participants (Mage=14.56, 75.0% female) completed the qualitative interview study, including 11 lifetime cannabis users. Two and four cannabis-using participants used the Gillick-competent pathway in the quantitative and qualitative studies, respectively. In the quantitative study, 38/175 participants (21.7%) triggered low-intensity signposting and one participant received additional safeguarding actions. Three qualitative participants received safeguarding actions. Both studies successfully elicited detailed information on cannabis use, mental health and contextual experiences.

Conclusion: We recruited nearly 200 13-15-year-old adolescent participants, including those who used cannabis, collected rich data about illegal cannabis use and mental health using in-depth surveys and interviews, while keeping participants safe. We therefore proved we can feasibly conduct research about cannabis in <16-year-olds in the UK.

articles_hidden.title: Capacity Limits in Cognitive Processing Reflect the Curse of Generalization
articles_hidden.authors: Steven M Frankland; Raja Marjieh; Marco Nurisso; Joseph Fluegemann; Taylor Webb; Giovanni Petri; Richard L. Lewis; Jonathan D. Cohen
articles_hidden.abstract:
The striking constraints of some human cognitive processes stand in stark contrast
to the near limitless capability of others. While we can acquire and flexibly use vast amounts
of information, the amount we can process at any one time is often stiflingly limited: for
example the number of items we can hold in working memory or the number of tasks that can
be performed at once. Here, we integrate ideas from information theory, cognitive science,
and neuroscience to offer a unified account of why processing is often so limited. We argue
that this reflects a fundamental tradeoff between generalization—how effectively existing
representations can be used in novel settings—and how many distinct representations can
be processed in parallel. Representations that best promote strong forms of generalization
— a characteristically human cognitive strength — come at the expense of surprisingly
strict limits in the number of items that can be processed at once, an equally characteristic
human weakness. We refer to this as the “curse of generalization.” We formulate this first in
information-theoretic terms, and then in process models, including a neural network model
of classic tasks used to demonstrate strict limits in human processing capacity. This tension
offers a potential explanation for a range of phenomena — from performance on the tasks on
which we focus, to representational learning and skill acquisition more broadly — as well
as the performance of modern machine learning architectures that exhibit generalization
capabilities comparable to humans.

articles_hidden.title: Value-based control over memory encoding and search
articles_hidden.authors: Sven Wientjes; Clay B. Holroyd; Sean Matthew Polyn
articles_hidden.abstract: Memory is an adaptive cognitive function that enables individuals to use past experiences to guide future behavior. Prior research has demonstrated that goal-relevant, or rewarded, items are remembered more effectively, but the underlying mechanisms—ranging from automatic neuromodulation to strategic elaboration—remain debated. In this study, we investigated how different reward structures influence the temporal organization of free recall in mixed-item lists. Rewards were administered either during item encoding or were contingent on successful later recall. Our behavioral results reveal a striking mid-list primacy effect: when rewards are contingent on later recall, participants disproportionately initiate search at the onset of rewarded subsequences, effectively treating reward shifts as privileged access points. To account for these findings, we developed a novel hierarchical Bayesian implementation of the context maintenance and retrieval (CMR) model of free recall. By fitting the model to individual recall sequences, we adjudicated between competing accounts of memory enhancement. Our results demonstrate that motivated memory relies on two key mechanisms: the strengthening of context-to-item associations and the strategic creation of accessible event boundaries. These findings suggest the primacy effect involves the strategic reinstatement of a privileged context rather than solely the enhanced encoding of early list items. With regard to executive control and event segmentation theories, this suggests that participants exercise fine-grained control over their mental context, perhaps through varying mnemonic techniques. We propose that motivated memory is not merely a product of enhanced associative binding, but also involves active, structured (re)organization of experience.

articles_hidden.title: Shared and distinct patterns of cortical network-level functional connectivity associated with child psychopathology dimensions
articles_hidden.authors: Lei Cao
articles_hidden.abstract: Improving current understanding of the neurobiological mechanisms underlying child mental disorders could inform the development of effective therapeutic interventions. The United States National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) advocates to study neural correlates of child psychopathology using dimensional approach. Using baseline data from 8,970 children aged 9-10 years (50.37% male) in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, I applied bifactor modeling to decompose Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) into one general psychopathology factor and three specific symptom factors (Conduct Problems, ADHD, Internalizing Problems) and studied the association of both shared and specific factors with cortical network-level functional connectivity using multivariate method aiming to delineate both shared and distinct patterns of functional organization associated with different child psychopathology. The result showed that increased general psychopathology was associated increase bottom-up processing of sensorimotor hand and auditory information and top-down processing of visual information; increased Conduct Problems showed increased cognitive neglect of visual and sensorimotor information and elevated sensorimotor and auditory network activities; increased ADHD showed sustained abnormality in both top-down and bottom-up processing of motor and auditory information; increased Internalizing Problems showed hyperactivities in cognitive control, top-down and bottom-up processing, visual information processing and hypoactivities in bottom-up processing of visual information and spatial navigation as well as maintaining spatial navigation. Sensitivity analysis including race yielded largely consistent result. Adjusting for socioeconomic status attenuated the associations with Conduct Problems and Internalizing Problems, whereas associations with General Psychopathology and ADHD remained robust. My findings offered novel insights into neurobiological mechanisms of different child psychopathology and suggested altered functional organization of the brain could serve as a potential biomarker for child mental disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Bioengineering an improved niche for neural stem cells
articles_hidden.authors: Yash Parikh
articles_hidden.abstract: Aging is one of the key drivers of cognitive decline and slowing neurogenesis. It is a major risk factor for neurodegenerative diseases. In the process of aging, neural stem cells stop proliferating at a high level, and the niche surrounding them begins to undergo extensive change. This large shift consists of vascular changes, lower growth factor signaling, higher stiffness and tension, and reduced cell-to-cell interactions. In research to date, in vitro models have not recreated a full neural stem cell niche while taking into account all of the previously listed factors. In this proposal, a bioengineered, 3D niche specifically designed to recreate the environment of a young neurogenic niche is constructed. The niche will have the stiffness of its hydrogel extracellular matrix tuned, growth factors added and co-culturing of glial cells with neural stem cells. The neural stem cells, from aged mice and from young mice, will be sowed into the target niche and two controls, which will be developed into organoid systems. Measurements of two neuronal proteins in these organoids will demonstrate how successful the bioengineered niche will be at restoring neurogenesis to aged neural stem cells. This work could show how much of age-related cognitive decline is driven by the surrounding niche rather than intrinsic issues with the cells. Additionally, a successful organoid would also be exceptionally useful for disease modeling and for modeling strategies to restore neurogenesis in the aging brain.

articles_hidden.title: Tuned by Experience: Auditory statistical regularities shape attentional prioritization across pitch and timbre
articles_hidden.authors: Jason A Davis; Douglas A Addleman; Kevin Ortego; Viola S. Störmer
articles_hidden.abstract: Listeners navigate complex acoustic environments by selectively attending to relevant sounds amid competing noise. This capacity is classically attributed to top-down goals and bottom-up salience, but recent work implicates a third influence: selection history, whereby incidental exposure to statistical regularities shapes attentional prioritization. We investigated how incidental experience of selecting specific acoustic features influences attentional prioritization across different levels of auditory processing. Participants listened to two concurrently presented sounds to detect a target that contained a brief temporal gap. Unbeknownst to the participants, during a learning phase, one sound was more likely to contain the target gap; in a subsequent testing phase all sounds were equally likely to be the target. Experiment 1 used pure tones of varying pitches, and Experiment 2 used instrument chords (piano, trumpet, guitar). Across both experiments, participants responded faster to high-probability targets during learning, indicating facilitated attentional selection based on the statistical regularities across different levels of acoustic representations. This response time advantage persisted robustly throughout the unbiased testing phase for Experiment 1, but less so for Experiment 2, suggesting that the persistence of experience-driven auditory attention may depend on the complexity of the learned feature. Overall, our findings parallel selection-history effects observed in vision, providing evidence that similar influences of incidental experience on attentional priors exist across sensory modalities.

articles_hidden.title: Formless affect and lifeless fluency: Two ideal types of expressive failure in narcissism
articles_hidden.authors: Shiyun Zhang Isabelle
articles_hidden.abstract: Searches for narcissism and expressive language disorder return almost nothing, and the reason is conceptual. Expressive language disorder is a developmental diagnosis of structural language, whereas the expressive difficulties linked to narcissism arise where affect meets pragmatic form. The evidence that does exist looks contradictory. Narcissism as a whole is unrelated to alexithymia, yet grandiose narcissism correlates negatively with it and samples that include vulnerable narcissism correlate positively. Speakers high in narcissism are judged persuasive when they talk and unpersuasive when they write. This review resolves both patterns with Weber's ideal-type method, extended by falsification. It also draws on Etzrodt's reading of anomie and alienation as opposites: "formless life" and "lifeless form." Two ideal types follow. Anomic expression is affect that does not reach a speakable form. It accentuates the vulnerable pole, where difficulty identifying feelings, suppression, and dysregulation turn into anger, blame, or withdrawal. Alienated expression is fluent form cut off from self-threatening affect and closed to revision. It accentuates the grandiose pole, where speech is credited and self-reports flatter. Affective empathy is reduced there while cognitive empathy is intact, and a self-promoting style persists after it stops paying. Shared antagonism impairs repair at both poles, and both fail on shame in opposite ways. Developmental language disorder enters as a distal marker that raises the risk of later personality disorder without a dose-response relation to severity. Seven propositions, each with a refutation condition, separate the types from structural, trait-only, and strategic-choice accounts.

articles_hidden.title: Does CBT change the brain? A systematic review of neuroimaging RCTs on anxiety disorders, depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Ioulia Kokka; Iraklis Mourikis
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is effective for anxiety disorders, depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), but the neurobiological mechanisms of change remain unclear. This systematic review synthesized neuroimaging evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to examine whether CBT can be considered a neurobiological intervention. Following PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420251239465), PubMed, Scopus and PsycInfo were searched for RCTs of CBT in adults with anxiety disorders, depression or OCD-spectrum disorders reporting pre- and post-treatment neuroimaging. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2, and findings were synthesized narratively. Seventeen RCTs were included (OCD = 5, anxiety disorders = 6, depression = 6), using task-based fMRI (n = 8), resting-state fMRI (n = 6), structural MRI (n = 2) or PET (n = 1). Changes after CBT involved emotional reactivity regions, prefrontal and frontoparietal control systems and their connectivity, with disorder-specific patterns: reduced threat reactivity in anxiety disorders, altered cognitive control networks in OCD, and altered mood-related, self-referential and reward connectivity in depression. Neural and clinical change did not always coincide, and comparisons with pharmacotherapy were mixed. Five studies were at high risk of bias. These findings provide preliminary support for CBT as a neurobiological intervention, although small samples and heterogeneous protocols limit conclusions.

articles_hidden.title: Tracking vocabulary development as children start school: assessing measurement invariance in multilingual classrooms
articles_hidden.authors: Sonali Nag; Athina Ntalli; Gideon Arulmani; Joshua Aaron McGrane
articles_hidden.abstract: Receptive vocabulary, what is understood when hearing a word, underpins reading comprehension and wider learning. Yet, few tests have been validated to function fairly over developmental time and across diverse linguistic experiences. This study examined the Picture Test for Receptive Vocabulary (TalkTogether – Hindi), a 50-item test for four-to-nine-year-olds in multilingual north India. Words in the language of school instruction and linked images were drawn picture- and story books. Over one academic year (2023–2024), 1,949 administrations were collected from children (47% girls) at three time points across 40 schools. The test showed good reliability (Cronbach’s α = .82; Rasch reliability = .78) and captured variation across the proficiency range. Item properties remained stable across time, licensing its use as a fair tracking tool. Between-group differential item functioning (DIF) effects—by sex, home language(s), and a novel index of ambient peer language exposure—were small to negligible. The findings demonstrate that a contextually-situated vocabulary test, validated through rigorous psychometric evaluation, can meet the standards required for fair tracking of oral skills in the language of instruction. The reported protocol to inform item revision and evaluate dimensions of measurement invariance—demographic, contextual and developmental—are likely transferable to other similarly multilingual settings.

articles_hidden.title: Mental Health Conditions as Processes: Developmental Features and Clinical Implications
articles_hidden.authors: Vadim Pérez Koldenkova
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental disorders are typically approached as syndrome-defined states, and questions like why conditions outlast their triggers, why diagnoses overlap, why some resist treatment, how change occurs and what recovery should aim at are usually addressed separately. Here, we approach mental health conditions as processes within a person’s lifelong development, putting forward four propositions: 1) maintenance and development compete for a limited capacity for change; 2) repeated activity becomes structure; 3) self-maintenance can turn into entrapment, which depletes finite reserves; 4) reorganization is often abrupt and lasts only if consolidated. From this perspective, mental health appears as the preserved capacity to keep developing, whereas many persistent conditions appear as active entrapment—a pattern reproduced by the person’s own activity (avoidance, rumination). Therefore, entering a state, remaining in it, leaving it and stabilizing the outcome can depend on different conditions. For each of these phases we derive clinical implications and testable predictions.

articles_hidden.title: Psychometric Refinement of the Cognitive Assessment in Music Therapy for Institutionalized Older Adults (ACPIM-5)
articles_hidden.authors: Mariana Lacerda Arruda; Frederico Gonçalves Pedrosa; Gislaine Cristina Vagetti
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: This study psychometrically refined the Cognitive Assessment of Older Adults in Music Therapy (ACPIM) and evaluated its convergent validity and longitudinal stability relative to the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). 
Method: Participants included 180 institutionalized older adults (mean age = 79.0 ± 8.2 years; 93.9% cognitively impaired). Psychometric refinement integrated Network Psychometrics, Rasch Partial Credit Modeling, and Confirmatory Factor Analysis. 
Results: MoCA items required category collapsing to resolve disordered thresholds. Refinement yielded a unidimensional 5-item scale (ACPIM-5) demonstrating adequate fit (χ²(4) = 4.039, p = 0.401; CFI = 1.000; TLI = 1.000; RMSEA = 0.007, 90% CI [0.000, 0.113]; ω = 0.896) and high fidelity with the 18-item version (r = 0.930). A bifactor model confirmed to be a dominant General Factor (H = 0.896; factor determinacy = 0.928) convergent with the MoCA (r = 0.380). ROC analysis demonstrated acceptable preliminary discrimination (AUC = 0.768, 95% CI [0.593, 0.943]; cutoff = 12.5; sensitivity = 72.8%; specificity = 81.8%).
Discussion: The ACPIM-5 satisfied 7-day metric invariance (Δχ²(5) = 3.418, p = 0.636), confirming factor loading equivalence. In contrast, the MoCA violated scalar invariance (Δχ²(20) = 43.896, p = 0.0015), indicating threshold drift. The ACPIM-5 provides a context grounded, rapid screening metric for music therapy with institutionalized older adults.

articles_hidden.title: A Multilevel Signal Detection Theory Approach to Unconscious Processing Research
articles_hidden.authors: Ricardo Rey-Sáez; Alicia Franco-Martínez; Miguel A. Vadillo; Francisco Garre-Frutos
articles_hidden.abstract: To test for unconscious processing, researchers typically compare measures of a stimulus’s influence on behavior with measures of awareness of that stimulus. Three common hypotheses are often tested: whether influence is significant while awareness is not (group-level dissociation), whether both measures are independent across participants (correlation), or whether influence persists when awareness is extrapolated to be zero (regression intercept). Conventional analyses suffer from three well-known methodological limitations: First, both measures often differ in scale and number of trials, complicating meaningful comparisons of their relative sensitivities. Second, analyses based on participant-level sensitivities ignore measurement error, which attenuates correlations and inflates regression intercepts, leading to misleading evidence for unconscious processing. Third, the correlation hypothesis requires evidence of null association, but conventional significance tests provide limited evidence for the absence of an effect. To address these problems, we introduce a multilevel signal detection theory (SDT) model that jointly analyzes trial-level responses from both measures and allows all three hypotheses to be tested directly while accounting for measurement error. The model supports both frequentist and Bayesian estimation, allowing researchers to run non-superiority tests and quantify evidence for null hypotheses using Bayes factors. We illustrate this approach through reanalyses of three published studies on unconscious processing. The {uSDT} R package provides an accessible way to fit the joint multilevel SDT model and evaluate all three hypotheses more rigorously.

articles_hidden.title: Linking Expectancies and Interpretations: A Transdiagnostic Mediation Model of Intolerance of Uncertainty
articles_hidden.authors: Elinor Abado; Julie Lin Ji; Julian Basanovic; Colin MacLeod; Anne Schacht; Marcella Lydia Woud
articles_hidden.abstract: Expectancy and interpretation biases are widely considered transdiagnostic markers of psychopathology, yet the nature of their relationship remains understudied. If these processes are causally related, modifying one may influence the other and reduce associated symptoms. Intolerance of uncertainty (IU) is a transdiagnostic trait linked to biased interpretations and their modification. The present study tested a mediation model in which interpretations were hypothesized to mediate the relationship between expectancies and IU. According to this account, expectancy-related ratings were expected to predict interpretation-related ratings, which in turn were expected to predict trait IU. In an online study, N = 263 unselected participants completed a novel task in which each trial paired an expectancy sentence and rating with a subsequent interpretation sentence and rating, jointly assessing both processes. Sentence valence (neutral/emotional) and expectancy-interpretation outcome pairings (e.g., positive-positive, positive-negative) varied randomly across trials. Results showed that more negative expectancy and interpretation ratings were associated with higher levels of trait IU, anxiety, and depression, whereas more positive ratings were associated with lower levels of each. In a cross-sectional mediation model, expectancies showed significant direct paths to both interpretations and IU, but interpretations did not mediate the expectancy-IU relationship. These findings point to a central transdiagnostic role for expectancies relative to interpretations. Interventions may therefore benefit from prioritizing expectancy biases; nonetheless, the observation that expectancy and interpretation biases were associated with symptom measures in opposing and complementary directions indicates that joint assessment of both cognitive processes remains more informative than assessing either alone.

articles_hidden.title: Auditory Working Memory Is Susceptible to Intrusions from Subsequent Sounds
articles_hidden.authors: Manda Fischer; Keisuke Fukuda
articles_hidden.abstract: As sounds unfold over time, listeners often need to relate successive events while keeping them distinct. Auditory working memory is susceptible to interference from subsequent sounds, yet whether resulting errors reflect distortion of the remembered target or intrusion of the intervening sound itself remains unclear. Although both mechanisms can produce similar average biases toward an intervening sound, they predict distinct distributions of reproduction errors. Recent advances in continuous pitch reproduction now allow us to test these predictions in audition. In two experiments, participants remembered a target tone over a brief delay and reproduced its pitch on a circular continuous-response scale. During the delay, an intervening tone was presented; participants either ignored it or judged its similarity to the target. We analyzed reproduction-error distributions with mixture modeling to distinguish systematic shifts in target-centred responses (i.e., distortion) from responses clustered around the intervening pitch (i.e., intrusion).  The results showed that the error distributions were better accounted for by models incorporating responses centred near the intervening pitch (i.e., intrusion) than the models assuming continuous displacement of target-centred responses alone (i.e., distortion). Exploratory analyses suggested that the influence of task relevance of the intervening sound was associated with baseline memory precision: listeners with less precise baseline reproduction tended to show greater interference when told to explicitly compare the sounds. Together, these findings suggest that intervening sounds may do more than bias reports of remembered pitch. On some trials, the intervening sound may guide the final response in place of the target, even when task-irrelevant.

articles_hidden.title: Can LLMs Grow Like Children? A Developmental Analysis of Capability Trajectories in Language Model Training
articles_hidden.authors: Ran An; Tingting Chung; Klaus Libertus
articles_hidden.abstract: Within two years, an infant who can barely lift her head learns to sit, reach, and walk. Developmental science found that this growth is both continuous and phased: skills improve smoothly, yet the pace of improvement changes at identifiable ages, and the field built statistical tools to locate those changes. Language models also transform across training, and whether their capabilities grow smoothly or in jumps is actively debated. The present study argues that the developmental answer applies to artificial learners as well, and that the developmental tools can show it. We apply an analysis pipeline built for infant motor development to the training trajectories of 16 open-source language models, each tested at 27 points during training on five benchmarks. The results mirror the infant findings. Growth is continuous but organized into phases, and transitions cluster at a small set of shared points that are deployed differently across domains. Growth proceeds slowly, then rapidly, then slowly, and models differ reliably in developmental rate. Unlike infants, those rate differences are almost entirely explained by model size. The transitions also survive changes of measurement scale, and on a continuous measure they appear earlier and more sharply than on accuracy. The paper contributes a formal test for phase structure in capability growth, a construct mapping between infant development and language model development, and evidence that phase structure may be a shared property of learning systems.

articles_hidden.title: Uncertainty Weighting as a Time-Invariant Principle of Crossmodal Inference
articles_hidden.authors: Manda Fischer; Keisuke Fukuda
articles_hidden.abstract: In a dynamic world, events unfold and disappear, often providing only fleeting or incomplete sensory evidence. Information from another sense may help us interpret these encounters, but what determines how strongly it influences what we later remember? Across two audiovisual working-memory experiments, we tested whether auditory context exerts greater influence when visual information is reconstructed less reliably. Participants viewed a face morphed along a feminine–masculine continuum for 100ms and, after a 1,900-ms retention interval, reproduced it using a continuous face-morph response wheel. On cue trials, a feminine- or masculine-sounding voice was presented 1,000ms before face onset (prediction) or 900ms after face offset (postdiction). In Experiment 1 (N=84), voice cues shifted reconstructions toward the cued gender in both tasks. Across observers, weaker visual sensitivity was associated with greater auditory influence; and within observers, faces reconstructed less consistently without cues showed stronger bias. Experiment 2 (N=170) extended this relationship to externally imposed visual uncertainty through resolution reduction and spatial occlusion. Across both manipulations and cue timings, less reliable reconstruction was associated with greater auditory cue influence. Despite this consistency in uncertainty-sensitive auditory influence, the way voices influenced reconstructions depended on whether they were heard before or after the face. Together, these findings suggest a recurring functional principle of crossmodal inference: The less reliably visual information can be reconstructed, the more strongly contextual information influences the resulting judgment. Differences in how auditory bias was expressed suggest prediction and postdiction may address the same inferential challenge through different underlying processes.

articles_hidden.title: Phronesis (Practical Wisdom) as a Measure of Moral Excellence:  A Comparative Study of Business and Non-Business Students at a Joint-Venture University in China
articles_hidden.authors: Yan Huo; Hyemin Han; Shane McLoughlin; Eddy Fang; Kristján Kristjánsson
articles_hidden.abstract: The present study compares mastery of phronesis (i.e., practical wisdom) between business school students and students in other schools at a joint-venture university in China. We inquired whether business students’ practical wisdom was more evident or less evident compared with the non-business students. Our question was motivated by the existing research in the business ethics literature that does not provide a ‘happy reading’ about business students, whose qualities are often associated with dishonesty, greed, corruption, and selfishness, more so than those of non-business students. We utilised the Short Phronesis Measure (SPM), which was recently developed and validated; it assesses moral functioning holistically, different from most conventional measures that focus only on individual traits or virtue/vice constructs. We collected data from 653 participants (business students, n=289; non-business students, n=364). Our Bayesian analysis of the data showed that business students’ phronesis mastery was not significantly different from that of non-business students in all domains. The finding suggests that business students are not inferior in phronetic moral functioning in general. This serves as an important reminder for business school educators that business students have the same potential as other students to achieve moral excellence.

articles_hidden.title: Color cues, developmental coupling, and the limits of the late-sighted model: A commentary on Vogelsang et al. (2024)
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract:
Vogelsang et al. (2024) report in Science that congenitally blind individuals who gain sight late in life rely disproportionately on color cues for object recognition, unlike normally sighted controls. They propose that this pattern reflects the adaptive value of neonatal color immaturity: because typical infants experience a period of degraded chromatic input, they develop object representations grounded in luminance rather than color.
The theoretical account, however, rests on an incomplete engagement with the developmental literature. Decades of research indicate that color and luminance sensitivity are developmentally coupled through shared photoreceptor immaturity: the same front-end bottleneck that degrades chromatic input in neonates simultaneously degrades luminance and spatial processing. If this coupling is real, there is no luminance-first window, because the bottleneck lifts for both dimensions together. The account's central premise is therefore undermined not by arguing independence, but by showing that color and luminance do not develop in the sequence the account requires.
I further identify methodological concerns: a small and unusual sample, a fixed order confound in the primary behavioral task, a computational model implementing a binary switch rather than the gradual chromatic cascade of normal development, and a color sensitivity test using non-equiluminant stimuli, leaving open the possibility that luminance rather than chromatic contrast sensitivity drove performance.
Together, these issues require qualification of the conclusions of Vogelsang et al. and reconciliation of the proposed account with classical findings in infant visual development. This broader question remains important, but the answer is unlikely to hinge on color alone.

articles_hidden.title: From Formal Theory to Personalized Treatment: A Precision Mental Health Roadmap
articles_hidden.authors: Nathaniel R Choukas; Sharina Hamm; Donald Robinaugh; Dawson Haddox; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Eiko I Fried; Denny Borsboom; Shirley B Wang; Zachary Daniel Cohen
articles_hidden.abstract: Evidence-based psychotherapies benefit many patients, but individual outcomes vary and guidance for personalizing treatment remains limited. The verbal theories underlying these treatments describe processes thought to produce improvement but often leave their strength, direction, functional form, and timescales unspecified. This limits theory-informed predictions about how a particular patient would respond to alternative treatments. Researchers have begun formalizing theories of psychopathology in mathematical or computational form to address these limitations. Formal theories make theoretical assumptions explicit, allowing precise and testable predictions to be deduced analytically or through computational models. When these models represent treatment effects and relevant individual differences, researchers can use patient measurements to inform model states and parameters, simulate alternative treatment configurations, and compare predicted outcomes. Empirical evaluation must distinguish the accuracy of outcome predictions, support for the proposed mechanisms, and whether model-guided selection or adaptation improves outcomes relative to other treatment selection strategies. Translating this potential into practice requires aligning the theory with patient assessment, treatment delivery, and evaluation. We propose a roadmap for this process and describe conditions supporting the generation, delivery, and testing of formal theory-driven treatment recommendations. A worked example using a formal theory of panic disorder and a modular digital therapy illustrates the roadmap’s early phases, including provisional model extensions that generate different treatment predictions for two simulated patients. We conclude by discussing challenges in theory development, patient matching, measurement, and empirical evaluation that must be addressed before these predictions can guide clinical care.

articles_hidden.title: The longitudinal relation between motor and language skills at two and four-to 4.5 years of age in a large Singaporean cohort
articles_hidden.authors: Naomi Havron; Hugo Peyre; Yap Seng Chong; Birit F.P. Broekman; Lourdes Mary Daniel; Shirong Cai; Sho Tsuji
articles_hidden.abstract: Early language is intricately related to the development of other skills. Motor skills, in particular, have been associated with language development, but the precise relations between these domains is a matter of ongoing research. Here we examined the longitudinal relations between fine- and gross-motor skills and language abilities in a large population cohort (N = 885, 49% female) from Singapore. Using a cross-lagged panel model with data from 9 to 48 months of age, we investigated both within-time associations and directional effects between motor and language domains. We found significant concurrent associations between motor and language skills. Fine-motor skills at 9 months predicted language development at 18 months, even after controlling for demographic factors. None of the other cross-domains paths was significant. In order to explain this discrepancy with past research, we therefore also explored without controlling for these factors. This latter  analysis revealed more predictive paths from gross and fin- motor to language development, from the age of 9 months up to two years, suggesting that previous findings might be explained by confounding factors. Our findings highlight the importance of controlling for confounding factors when examining the relation between motor and language development.

articles_hidden.title: Behavioral dimensions and white matter organization in early childhood following preterm birth
articles_hidden.authors: Sakshi Kaur; David Vanier; Dennis Dimond; Kirk Graff; Ryann Tansey; Amanda Ip; Shelly Yin; Daria Merrikh; Christiane Rohr; Lily Koochak
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Children born preterm are at increased risk for attentional, social and emotional challenges, collectively referred to as the preterm behavioral phenotype. While white matter alterations have been linked to individual behavioral domains following preterm birth, it remains unclear whether distinct dimensions of behavioral variability are associated with specific patterns of white matter organization. Understanding neurobiological risk markers for preterm phenotypic traits may help identify children at greatest risk. 
Objective: We investigated the extent to which these behavioral traits covary across the gestational age spectrum and whether latent behavioral dimensions are associated with white matter micro- and macro-structure in young children born preterm. 
Methods: We collected behavioral and diffusion MRI data from 58 children born preterm (29 females; mean age = 5.64 ± 0.99 years; GA range = 24-36 weeks) and 85 full-term children aged 4-8 years (44 females; mean age = 5.91 ± 0.95 years; mean GA = 39.26 ± 1.24 weeks). Principal component analyses were performed separately in preterm, full-term, and combined groups to characterize latent behavioral dimensions spanning autism-related traits, ADHD symptoms, and emotional functioning. Fixel-based analysis was then used to examine associations between behavioral dimensions and fiber density and fiber cross-section, adjusting for demographic and perinatal factors.
Results: In the preterm sample, autism- and ADHD-related behaviors emerged as relatively distinct dimensions, whereas behavioral variance in the full-term sample was captured by a broad neurodevelopmental dimension. In children born preterm, higher scores on the ADHD-related behavioral dimension were associated with reduced fiber cross-section in the splenium of the corpus callosum. No significant associations were found for fiber density in the preterm or full-term samples. 
Conclusions: These findings suggest that prematurity influences not only behavioral outcomes, but also how those outcomes relate to white matter organization, highlighting the importance of considering behavioral heterogeneity when investigating brain-behavior relationships in preterm populations.

articles_hidden.title: Failure to distinguish “mental health” from “mental illness” disrupts effective policy for population well-being
articles_hidden.authors: Kai Ruggeri; Hannes Jarke; Sofia Pelica
articles_hidden.abstract: The semantics and measurement of “mental health”, “well-being”, and “mental illness” have long been debated - as has the way clinicians and policymakers are expected to respond to their associated insights. However, despite existing discussion on distinctions between these terms, there is an urgent need to more forcefully articulate how key terminology in mental health should be used. Failures to do so have been problematic and directly impacted how mental health is understood, which has subsequently impacted efforts to prevent and treat mental illness as well as protect and promote mental health. Here we highlight significant concerns about incorrect use of these terms, their implications, and why the field needs to urgently apply more stringency in the literature. Our aim is not to criticize journals, articles, or authors for such mixing, but rather to provide compelling arguments as to why it is critical to be correct and precise about how these are discussed, measured, and addressed to benefit population well-being.

articles_hidden.title: The Dark Triad and trait aggression in women and men: Clarifying the substantive consequences of factor overlap
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolás González-Raposo; Pablo Polo; Eduardo Galaz Villarroel; Katrin Schaefer; Bernhard Fink; Todd K. Shackelford; Virgil Zeigler-Hill; Tobias Koch; Ulrich S. Tran; Jose Antonio Muñoz Reyes
articles_hidden.abstract: Although the Dark Triad (i.e., psychopathy, Machiavellianism, and narcissism) has been consistently linked to aggressive behaviors such as bullying and violence, two important questions about these associations remain unresolved. First, little is known about how they differ between women and men. Second, it remains unclear how factor overlap affects their substantive interpretation. Drawing on evolutionary accounts of intrasexual competition, we predict stronger associations with physical and verbal aggression in men and hostility in women. We test these predictions on Short Dark Triad and Buss and Perry Aggression Questionnaire data from 600 Chilean adults, using bifactor (S−1) structural equation modeling. We find that Machiavellianism predicts all aggression outcomes, psychopathy-specific variance positively predicts physical aggression, and narcissism-specific variance negatively predicts hostility. Sex differences in aggression overlap with sex differences in aversive traits, but none of the Dark Triad-aggression associations consistently differ by sex. By introducing the variance-weighted latent effect (VWLE), we provide the first substantive translation of these bifactor associations. VWLE clarifies how reference facet and trait-specific associations reinforce one another for psychopathy but largely cancel out for narcissism, making the implications of residual coefficients explicit.

articles_hidden.title: Menstrual Cycle Status and the Acute Subjective Psychedelic Experience
articles_hidden.authors: Alaina Srivastav; Sunjuri Sun; Peter Hendricks; Walter Osika; Cecilia Ulrika Dagsdotter Stenfors; Sankalp Chaturvedi; Michelle Olofsson; Gabriella Smedfors; Simon Goldberg; Otto Simonsson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Individual differences shape the acute subjective psychedelic experience, but menstrual cycle status remains an understudied source of potential variability.
Methods: In a longitudinal observational study, 169 participants reported psychedelic use during the two-month study period. Participants were classified by menstrual cycle status during their most intense psychedelic experience: menstruating during the experience (n=15), menstruating but not during the experience (n=60), not menstruating (n=25), and male participants (n=69). Primary analyses examined associations between cycle status and ego dissolution (Ego Dissolution Inventory; EDI), mystical-type experience (Mystical Experience Questionnaire; MEQ), and challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire; CEQ), adjusting for dose and age. Exploratory analyses examined MEQ and CEQ subscales and post-acute risk of harm to self and others.
Results: Participants menstruating during their experience reported higher EDI scores than both those menstruating but not during the experience and male participants (β=−0.89 and −0.68, ps≤.011). Cycle status was not associated with MEQ or CEQ scores. Exploratory analyses found higher physical distress and death subscale scores among participants menstruating during their experience than among those menstruating but not during the experience (β=−0.77 and −0.80, ps≤.005). Risk of post-acute harm to self and others was higher among those menstruating during the experience than among those menstruating regularly but not during the experience (OR=6.41, p=.022).
Conclusions: Menstrual cycle timing may be associated with aspects of the acute psychedelic experience, specifically ego dissolution and potentially risk of post-acute harm to self and others. These preliminary findings support further investigation of menstrual cycle status in psychedelic research.

articles_hidden.title: Gender-Inclusive Voice and Communication Training: Supporting Nonbinary Clients
articles_hidden.authors: Maura Philippone; Thea Knowles; Becks von Duering
articles_hidden.abstract: Nonbinary clients may pursue gender-affirming voice training (GAVT) goals that extend beyond traditional masculinization and feminization goals. This clinical perspective discusses potential applications of existing clinical frameworks for nonbinary clients, with particular focus on meta-therapy and the Acoustic Assumptions (AA) as gender-inclusive approaches. These approaches support gender-inclusive, person-centered exploration of voice and communication characteristics while drawing on established principles of speech production. Although further research is needed to establish more gender-inclusive acoustic and perceptual outcome measures, clinicians can presently use customizable, person-centered approaches to support diverse GAVT goals and provide affirming care.

articles_hidden.title: SaccadeJS: Webcam eye tracking for behavioral experiments in a web browser
articles_hidden.authors: Joshua R de Leeuw; Colin Mikulski; Alex Teabo; Cherrie Chang
articles_hidden.abstract: Webcam eye tracking allows researchers to study eye movements in large, geographically diverse online samples, but its accuracy has limited it to coarse comparisons, such as which half or quadrant of the screen a participant is looking at. We introduce SaccadeJS, an open-source webcam eye tracker that runs entirely in the participant's browser. SaccadeJS uses a neural network to transform images of the eyes to features, which a ridge regression maps to screen positions. The network can be rapidly calibrated by computing new regression weights on a sample of fixations at known locations. To train the model, we collected a new dataset of 2,003 participants who fixated targets on their own laptop and desktop computers. In a validation study with 200 new online participants, the median participant's error was about 4% of the screen diagonal. That accuracy is enough to distinguish many more, and smaller, areas of interest than halves and quadrants. We also developed a timing calibration routine to measure each participant's camera lag. After correction, saccade latencies matched distributions from laboratory experiments. We report how different calibration strategies and image characteristics affect accuracy. SaccadeJS could be run in real time on about one third of the participants in the validation study; for others, the library processes frames in the background while the experiment runs. SaccadeJS can be used as standalone software for webcam eye tracking or in conjunction with jsPsych through a set of provided plugins for calibration, validation, and recording.

articles_hidden.title: The control limit hypothesis of schizophrenia
articles_hidden.authors: Georg Keller; Philipp Sterzer
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the last half century, we have made little progress in the treatment of schizophrenia. A key contributor to this is an insufficient understanding of what is causing the disorder. There are currently two broad families of hypotheses: those focused on a dopaminergic dysfunction, and those focused on a glutamatergic dysfunction. Based on recent findings that antipsychotic drugs exhibit cell-type specific and long-term effects on cortical circuit function, we integrate the two hypotheses into what we call the control limit hypothesis of schizophrenia. It builds on the assumption that schizophrenia is the result of a developmental miswiring of cortical circuits that is based on glutamatergic dysfunction and causes aberrant cortical activity dynamics. These cortical alterations likely underlie cognitive dysfunction, one of the core treatment-resistant symptoms of schizophrenia. The control limit hypothesis further postulates that the brain responds to and can partially mitigate these aberrant cortical dynamics by increasing dopamine levels in the striatum. When this regulatory system is driven to a control limit and dopamine levels exceed a given threshold, psychosis emerges. Beyond explaining much of the existing data, the hypothesis makes several predictions about cortical function testable in mice and humans.

articles_hidden.title: Neural responses to socioemotional information are more similar among siblings and relate to social competence
articles_hidden.authors: Sofia Scatolin; Elena Federici; Plamina Dimanova; Dennis Saikkonen; Jonathan Bugmann; Nora Maria Raschle
articles_hidden.abstract:
Socioemotional skills are fundamental to children’s well-being and development, yet the
neurodevelopmental processes through which familial relationships contribute to these skills
remain poorly understood. While socioemotional skills are partly heritable, they are also shaped by
social learning through interactions with others, including siblings. Sibling relationships represent
one of the earliest and most enduring social contexts throughout development and provide a
valuable context for investigating how familial relatedness is reflected in children's neural
processing of socioemotional information. However, little is known about whether siblings exhibit
similarities in these neural responses and how such similarities relate to socioemotional behavior.
In this study, we investigated whether sibling dyads show greater similarity in neural responses
during socioemotional processing than unrelated child dyads and whether such neural similarity is
associated with socioemotional functioning. To assess this, 120 children (6-14 years), including 39
sibling dyads, completed a naturalistic fMRI movie-watching task designed to elicit socioemotional
responses. Results showed that sibling dyads exhibited greater whole-brain functional neural
similarity during socioemotional processing than unrelated children across the whole brain. Region-
of-interest analyses further revealed greater functional neural similarity among siblings across
several prefrontal, temporal, and limbic regions, including the left ventromedial prefrontal cortex
(vmPFC). Moreover, greater similarity in left vmPFC responses, a region implicated in social
cognition, was associated with higher levels of socially competent behavior in both sibling and
unrelated dyads, suggesting that neural similarity may be particularly pronounced among children
with higher social competence. These findings highlight sibling relationships as an informative
context for investigating familial similarities in neural responses to socioemotional information and
their associations with socioemotional behavior during childhood.

articles_hidden.title: How to Design a Panel Study for Investigating Bivariate Dynamics Using Continuous-Time Modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Nuria Real-Brioso; Eduardo Estrada
articles_hidden.abstract: Designing effective longitudinal panel studies to capture bivariate dynamics requires making informed decisions about how many measurements to collect and when to collect them. This study examines how design choices, concretely sample size, number of repeated measures, and various aspects of the temporal sampling schedule, influence the recovery of bivariate dynamic parameters in panel data analyzed using a Continuous-Time Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (CT-RI-CLPM). Through a Monte Carlo simulation, we tested a range of generating population parameters. We proposed a novel approach for planning sampling schedules: the Short-and-Long Lags design (SHALL) which deliberately mixes closely spaced and widely spaced intervals that continuous time models can accommodate.
