SHALL schedules are simple to understand and implement, and consistently ranked among the best sampling schedules in many scenarios. Our findings suggest that the number of repeated measurements and sample size significantly impact parameter recovery, particularly for cross-lagged effects, which exhibited low estimation efficiency even in the most favorable conditions, leading to low statistical power. We provide actionable recommendations for researchers planning panel data studies, along with open-source R code to facilitate the design of SHALL sampling schedules. We also provide R code to implement a CT-RI-CLPM to new data sets. An empirical example illustrates the application of such a model to data from an empirical panel study relating self-esteem and depression. This work contributes evidence-based guidance for improving the design and analysis of longitudinal panel studies using continuous-time modeling.

articles_hidden.title: Getting ready for minority language transmission: Language management preparation among expecting parents in Fryslân
articles_hidden.authors: Suzanne Victoria Dekker; Jelske Dijkstra; Pavlina Heinzova; Mirjam Vellinga; Ruth Kircher
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines a previously unexplored aspect of family language policies: namely how expecting parents prepare for language management, focusing on their engagement with language-related resources – books, leaflets, magazines, etc. – to support them in getting ready to raise their children (bi-/multilingually) with a minority language. We collected questionnaire data from 520 participants in the province of Fryslân, the Netherlands. The majority language of the Netherlands is Dutch; Fryslân is home to most speakers of the minority language Frisian. Quantitative data were analysed statistically, qualitative data were analysed using conventional qualitative content analysis. Findings show that most participants decided what language(s) to transmit prior to pregnancy. Furthermore,  expecting parents who ultimately ended up transmitting Frisian were more aware of, and used more, resources than parents who ultimately did not transmit Frisian. The former also indicated a desire for additional resources to support bilingual (Dutch-Frisian) child-rearing and Frisian transmission. The paper discusses the study’s implications for policy and planning aiming to promote the intergenerational transmission of Frisian, and thereby promoting its maintenance and revitalisation.

articles_hidden.title: Not passive sponges: When attention wanes, our brains are less synchronized with the environment
articles_hidden.authors: Elena Greatti; Laura Batterink; Davide Crepaldi; Amy Finn
articles_hidden.abstract: Without even being aware, humans are amazingly sensitive to the structures around them. Is this sensitivity constant or does it fluctuate along with our attentional states? To answer this foundational question, we deployed temporally sensitive measures that allow us to track neural entrainment—the synchronization of brain activity to environmental regularities—alongside fluctuations in attentional states. Participants (n = 78) viewed both random and structured visual streams while performing a task to index fluctuating attentional states. Structured streams evoked robust neural entrainment and reduced attentional lapses. Moreover, attentional states varied with neural entrainment. Across participants, those who displayed greater neural entrainment had reduced attentional lapses. And critically, even within individuals, greater entrainment was observed during periods of greater attentional focus. Our sensitivity to structure and attentional states are therefore inextricably linked: structures stabilize our attentional states and our sensitivity to structure dynamically mirrors the ebb and flow of human attention.

articles_hidden.title: The Role of Musical Mood Regulation for Efficacy Beliefs and Hope in the Climate Crisis
articles_hidden.authors: Friederike Koehler; Dana Swarbrick; Suvi Saarikallio
articles_hidden.abstract:
Climate change is associated with a range of emotional responses, yet little is known about 
the role of music in regulating climate-related emotions and supporting adaptive 
psychological outcomes. Because music is widely used to regulate emotions and can foster 
positive affect, emotional coping, and resilience, it may also help individuals maintain hope 
when confronting the challenges of climate change. The present study examined whether 
music-based mood regulation of climate emotions is associated with hope, and whether this 
relationship is mediated by climate efficacy beliefs. A cross-sectional online survey was 
completed by 310 adults. Participants reported their use of music to regulate climate-
related emotions, climate efficacy beliefs (self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, collective 
efficacy, and collective outcome expectancy), and hope. Relationships among the variables 
were examined using correlation analyses and structural equation modeling. Several music-
based regulation strategies, particularly solace, diversion, strong sensation, and revival, 
were positively associated with hope. Some regulation strategies were also positively 
associated with self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, and collective outcome expectancy, 
whereas no significant bivariate associations emerged with collective efficacy. Structural 
equation modeling indicated a significant total indirect effect of music-based regulation on 
hope through climate efficacy beliefs. However, only self-efficacy and collective efficacy 
emerged as significant mediators. Outcome expectancy and collective outcome expectancy 
did not significantly mediate the association. The direct association between music-based 
regulation and hope remained significant, indicating partial mediation. These findings 
suggest that individuals who use music to regulate climate-related emotions report greater 
hope and that this association is partly explained by stronger perceptions of personal and 
collective capability. Climate efficacy beliefs emerged as a small yet significant pathway 
linking music-based regulation and hope. Music may therefore represent an accessible 
everyday resource that supports adaptive engagement with climate emotions and fosters 
hope in the context of climate change.

articles_hidden.title: Reading from childhood to adolescence: enduring influences of home environment on behaviour, motivation and proficiency
articles_hidden.authors: Sanne W van der Kleij; Jessie Ricketts; Laura Shapiro
articles_hidden.abstract: According to theoretical models of reading engagement, reading behaviours and reading motivation both influence reading proficiency. Additionally, annual surveys of young people’s reading engagement show decreasing numbers of children who report enjoying reading over time and across ages, but we lack longitudinal evidence confirming this decline. To examine the complex interaction between reading motivation, reading behaviour and reading proficiency, this study investigated: i) how young people’s motivation to read and reading behaviours change from age 10 to 15; ii) whether their engagement with reading is shaped by the home literacy environment (HLE); and iii) whether young people’s motivation to read determines their reading behaviours, in turn promoting reading comprehension. Data from a longitudinal study in [Blinded], UK (n = 598, 285 girls) were used to model the influence of HLE, reading motivation and reading behaviour on reading comprehension skills. Reading motivation, reading behaviour (i.e. time spent reading) and reading comprehension were assessed from age 10 to 15 and HLE was assessed in a subsample at age 11 (n = 299). Growth models showed that reading motivation and time spent reading declined from 11 to 13 years and then stabilised from age 14-15. However, trajectories of change differed across sex and socioeconomic status. In mediation models, the home literacy environment at age 11 was associated with children’s own reading engagement and showed direct and indirect associations with children’s reading comprehension outcomes. Our findings highlight the crucial influence of reading motivation on reading outcomes and uncover a longer-term role of HLE than previously assumed, extending well beyond childhood.

articles_hidden.title: Goals, Predictions, Valence: A Model Comparison of Agency Emergence
articles_hidden.authors: Jonas Richter; Marcel Raphael Schreiner
articles_hidden.abstract: The sense of agency (SoA), our feeling of control over actions and their environmental effects, has been explained through different theoretical models. This study compares three: the comparator model, proposing that SoA emerges from matching motor-based predictions to perceptual feedback, the ideomotor model, proposing that SoA emerges from monitoring goal achievement, and a self-serving bias model, proposing that SoA reflects self-attribution of positive and external attribution of negative outcomes. Participants performed a target-hitting task with manipulated visual feedback of positive or negative valence and rated their SoA on a subset of trials. The three models predict different SoA patterns based on motor activity appropriateness, goal achievement, and outcome valence. The ideomotor model best fit the empirical data, outperforming both alternatives, whereas evidence for an additional effect of outcome valence was ambiguous. These findings question the dominant role of motor-based predictions in SoA emergence and highlight goal achievement as a key determinant of SoA.

articles_hidden.title: Invariant agreement attraction effects: Distance and RC modification manipulations in Czech
articles_hidden.authors: Radim Lacina; Jakub Dotlacil
articles_hidden.abstract: Agreement attraction in comprehension often manifests itself as a speed-up in the of processing ungrammatical sentences where a verb carries the wrong number feature when a noun of the verb-matching number —the attractor—intervenes. The effect has been claimed to be insensitive to increased linear distance between the attractor and the agreement target. Recent studies on Czech found weak attraction effects attested only with case syncretic attractors. In two self-paced reading experiments with Czech comprehenders, we tested whether including material between the attractor and the verb could modulate attraction depending on whether the material was reinforcing the attractor's features or not. In Experiment 1, we aimed to increase attraction strength by modifying the attractor with a relative clause, giving it the subject feature and reinforcing its plurality. In Experiment 2, we matched the increased distance employed in Experiment 1 with feature-inert material to see if attraction was maintained. Our Bayes factor analysis provided us with evidence of a small attraction effect in the both experiments that did not differ meaningfully between the two. We therefore show that Czech exhibits online number attraction but of a tiny effect size. Our results further replicate earlier findings that distance does not affect agreement attraction in comprehension, as our effect sizes were comparable between the two experiments as well with previous work on Czech. Finally, they show that modifying attractors with relative clauses does not increase the strength of attraction speed-ups.

articles_hidden.title: On Bias in Detecting Bias: A Signal Detection Analysis of Attributions to Gender Discrimination
articles_hidden.authors: Marie Jakob; Anat Shechter; Jimmy Calanchini; Karl Christoph Klauer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Discrimination is the unjust treatment of people based on their group membership, and detecting discrimination is a necessary first step in countering it. Attributions to discrimination have often been conceptualized in terms of Signal Detection Theory (SDT), with researchers speculating about the role of sensitivity (i.e., observers’ ability to recognize discrimination) and response bias (i.e., their tendency to judge that discrimination is present) in observers’ judgments. Here, we take a first step toward moving beyond conceptual applications to empirical SDT analyses of attributions to
discrimination across five studies examining judgments about gender discrimination in corporate pay raise decisions. We find that prototypes (Studies 1 to 3) and their alignment with the actual pattern of decisions (Studies 2 to 4) inform observers’ response bias, reflecting differences in their attribution of unfair outcomes to discrimination (Study 5). In contrast, the extent of harm caused by discriminatory outcomes exerts a small effect on sensitivity and a large effect on response bias (Studies 1 to 3), which reflects observers’ determination of a fair standard for decisions (Study 5). Theoretically, the present work contributes to the causal analysis of central factors shaping attributions to discrimination. Specifically, we shed light on whether effects of these factors are mediated by response bias or sensitivity, and assess their causal origin in either the application of a merit standard or attributional processing.

articles_hidden.title: Development Insights and User Experience of a Preventive Digital Parenting Intervention for Adolescent Mental Health
articles_hidden.authors: Rick van Logchem; Crystal R. Smit; Anne Bülow; Hanneke Scholten; Bart Soenens; Loes Keijsers
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Despite being hailed as a promising avenue for preventing increasingly prevalent adolescent mental health problems, digital parenting interventions to strengthen adolescent mental well-being remain scarce. How such interventions are developed and experienced by end-users provides key insights for their later implementation and contextualizes information on their effectiveness, yet little systemic evidence is available.
Objective: To inform optimal development and aid careful evaluation of digital parenting interventions, this preregistered multimethod study served three aims. First, to identify theoretical, functional, and user-derived lessons for digital parenting interventions for adolescent mental well-being, distilled from the challenges of developing a novel digital parenting intervention. Second, to examine user experience in terms of feasibility, adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness as early markers of implementation success. Third, to understand whether user experience is linked to characteristics of the intervention (i.e., universal versus personalized delivery), parents (e.g., openness to advice), or adolescents (e.g., depressive symptoms).
Methods: Development of the intervention was based on Self-Determination Theory and followed an iterative process, including focus groups with parents and adolescents, a pilot study among n = 12 families and subsequent exit-interviews, and a brainstorm session with experts (n = 6). The intervention was evaluated among parents (N = 199, Mage = 47.6, SDage = 4.7), resulting in administrative and daily diary data of user experience (feasibility, adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness). Baseline data were used to test whether intervention, parent, and adolescent characteristics related to user experience.
Results: Findings suggest that adolescent perspectives align with the tenets of self-determination theory as a framework that can be translated to concrete advice for parents, that the frequency and delivery of advice should fit family routines, and parental agency and choice were important user needs. Feasibility, adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness were sufficient according to our preregistered criteria, but there was substantial heterogeneity between parents and within parents (across days). User experience did not differ between a personalized and universal version of the intervention. Parents who were generally more open to advice, and parents of boys, younger adolescents, and less depressed adolescents evaluated the intervention more favorably. 
Conclusions: Findings suggest that the fit between our intervention and parents differed substantially across parents, and from tip tot tip, highlighting the need for further refinement of our digital parenting interventions before implementation, and the consideration of user experience throughout development.

articles_hidden.title: Designing Around the Human Creative Core: A Construct for Preserving Creative Agency in Human-AI Systems
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract: Generative AI can increasingly perform the parts of professional work where a person's judgment and sense of identity are most engaged. The common design instinct is to automate wherever AI can plausibly take over, treating capability as the test. This efficiency-first instinct can erode the skill, judgment, ownership, and professional identity. Human-Centered AI frameworks show how to structure collaboration and keep people in control, but not which elements of a given workflow sustain a person's creative agency. This paper introduces the Human Creative Core: the subset of workflow elements where a person's cognitive contribution and psychological investment converge, identified through four dimensions, strategic intention, signature judgment, identity and ownership, and developmental function. The construct yields a design principle, complement the core and automate the periphery, and a method for locating the core in a given workflow. The method was taught and applied in a graduate instructional design course, and is demonstrated here across five professional cases. The contribution is a design construct and a repeatable method for building AI that preserves, and can strengthen, a person's creative agency rather than dissolving it.
